One of the most important persons associated with Kamianets-Podilskyi is Ivan Ohienko. The child nurtured by him in the most difficult conditions of 1918-1920 — Kamianets-Podilskyi State Ukrainian University — became the first center of Ukrainian education, science, and culture in Podillia. Both of the current universities operating in the city — Kamianets-Podilskyi State University and Podilskyi State Agrarian and Technical University — derive their lineage from Ohienko’s brainchild: the first — from the university opened on October 22, 1918, the second — from the one opened in the same University on October 22, 1919, Faculty of Agriculture. And if today Kamianets-Podilskyi is rightly called a university city, then the primary merit in this is one of the founders and the first rector of Kamianets-Podilskyi State Ukrainian University, Ivan Ohienko.

Gordian Knot. The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lw w) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian flags appeared on government offices and announcements circulated the city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic ( established with Lviv as its capital. For those Leopolitans who dreamed of a free Poland, the prospect of becoming West Ukrainian citizens was unac ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and increased desires to actively oppose these developments. That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting, giving rise to the legend of the Lw w Eaglets. On November 22, 191 due to resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left Lviv. This was, however, only the beginning of the Polish-Ukrainian war, or rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war. By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units went on the offensive. Partial forces from General J zef Haller’s army, which had arrived from France, were used for this purpose (though promises had been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in Galicia). Polish pressure forced the bleeding units to retreat behind the Zbruch River, which was to form the southeastern border of a reborn Poland. The last units crossed over on July 16, 1919. The government led by Yevhen Petrushevych went first to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and then into exile. The incorporation of the into the Polish Republic was accepted by the leader of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Symon Petliura, who wanted thereby to save Ukrainian statehood on the Dnieper River.

As is known, his hopes were dashed by the unfolding of the Polish-Soviet War and the Peace of Riga signed in March 1921.

Despite military defeat, western Ukrainians did not lose hope for indepen dence. The Poles had trouble getting the victorious powers, mainly France and England, to agree to Poland’s incorporation of Eastern Galicia. In June 1919 Poland was granted only the right of temporary administration over the region, while serious consideration was given to the idea that its fate should be decided by inhabitants themselves in a plebiscite held under the auspices of the League of Nations. Though Lviv was a Polish city, Ukrainians were the majority in the remainder of Eastern Galicia. According to the 1931 census, Lviv was inhabited by 157,000 Poles, 99,000 Jews, and just under 50,000 Ukrainians, yet of the 4,729,515 people living in all of Eastern Galicia, 2,847,844 were Greek Catholics (almost entirely Ukrainians), 1,350,978 declared themselves to be Roman Catholics (Poles), and 490,459 professed Judaism (Jews). The results of any plebiscite would have therefore certainly been unfavourable for Poland. The authorities of the Second Polish Republic, realizing this danger, began to strengthen Polish identity in the Kresy (Polish for “borderlands”) imme diately following the victory. Government offices were first to be Polonized, with all individuals refusing to swear an oath of allegiance to the Polish state being removed. Next, the Ukrainian chairs at the University of Lviv were abol ished and a principle by which only those Polish citizens who had served in the Polish Army could study there was adopted. Finally, on December 5, 1920, all of Galicia was divided into four voivodeships (provinces): Krak w, Lw w,

Tarnopol, and Stanisł w. The borders of these provinces were shifted west ward to change their demographic composition in favour of the Polish popula tion. Thus, Lw w Voivodeship came to include powiats (counties) inhabited mainly by Poles: Rzesz w, Kolbuszowa, Krosno, and Tarnobrzeg. Eastern Galicia was officially named Eastern Lesser Poland (Wschodnia Małopolska Moreover, in December 1920 the Legislative Sejm (Poland’s parliament) passed a law that granted farmsteads in Volhynia on favourable financial terms to deserving soldiers and war invalids from central Poland, who were often set tled in isolated settlements. These actions provoked opposition from a large portion of the Ukrainian population. The Ukrainian political parties did not recognize Polish statehood, accepting only the exiled government as a legal authority. A similar position was taken, among others, by the leader of the Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytskyi. A call for passive resistance went out, namely in the form of boycotts of the census being organized by the Polish authori ties, conscription into the army, and elections to the Sejm (November 1922). In October 1919 circles of underground Ukrainian education began forming, and July 1921 an underground university (existing until 1925) opened its doors.

The transfer of farms to Polish colonists was particularly resented – local peas ants commonly believed that the colonists appropriated land that should belong to them instead. The Ukrainians by no means intended to limit themselves to passive resis tance. Some Ukrainian officers and soldiers refused to lay down arms. In the summer of 1920, the underground Ukrainian Military Organization (UVO) was formed, headed by Colonel Yevhen Konovalets. The name of the organization rather inadvertently alluded to the Polish Military Organization ( bers of the UVO would later use Polish experiences in the struggle for inde pendence as a touchstone. Initially, UVO subordinated itself to Petrushevych’s government-in-exile in Vienna. Immediately after its creation, the organization began operations aimed at opposing the incorporation of Eastern Galicia and other disputed territories into the Republic of Poland. The first UVO terrorist act was carried out on November 25, 1921, in Lviv: an unsuccessful attempt on Marshal J zef Piłsudski’s life (with the accompanying Lviv Voivode Kazimierz Grabowski being wounded). Sabotage actions carried out under Konovalets’ direct leadership in the summer and autumn of 1922 were more serious. Grain stacks and farms of newly settled colonists and other Poles were set on fire. Bombs were planted at police and railroad stations, military warehouses, and on telegraph and telephone poles. Operations included the burning of mili tary warehouses near Przemyśl and police buildings in Yavoriv, Grdek, Uhniv and Lubacz w. As part of a liquidation of “traitors”, on October 15, 1922, in Kamianka Strumilova ( day UVO members killed Sydir Tverdohlib, a Ukrainian poet and journalist, leader of the Agrarian Ukrainian Peasants’ Party and candidate for the Polish Sejm. This sabotage campaign, supported by communist circles, lasted several months. Three hundred acts of sabotage and diversion were likely committed. Police statistics list 223 acts of sabotage in 1922, including 17 attacks on officials (with five killed), 15 attacks on Ukrainian conciliators (nine deaths), 129 acts of arson and robberies, 27 sabotages of state facilities, and 35 telephone and telegraph wire cutting incidents.

All this, however, failed to alter the Ukrainians’ position on the international stage. On March 14, 1923, the Council of Ambassadors, which had succeeded the Supreme War Council at the Paris Peace Conference, granted Eastern Galicia to Poland with the expectation that the local government of these ter ritories would be given certain autonomous rights. The decision of the Council of Ambassadors seemed to close the issue of Poland’s eastern border, at least in the perception of most western Ukrainians. This quickly eroded the authority of the Petrushevych government, with which even the UVO ceased coopera tion in its determination to continue its desperate struggle.

Tarnopol, and Stanisł w. The borders of these provinces were shifted west ward to change their demographic composition in favour of the Polish popula tion. Thus, Lw w Voivodeship came to include powiats (counties) inhabited mainly by Poles: Rzesz w, Kolbuszowa, Krosno, and Tarnobrzeg. Eastern Galicia was officially named Eastern Lesser Poland (Wschodnia Małopolska Moreover, in December 1920 the Legislative Sejm (Poland’s parliament) passed a law that granted farmsteads in Volhynia on favourable financial terms to deserving soldiers and war invalids from central Poland, who were often set tled in isolated settlements. These actions provoked opposition from a large portion of the Ukrainian population. The Ukrainian political parties did not recognize Polish statehood, accepting only the exiled government as a legal authority. A similar position was taken, among others, by the leader of the Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytskyi. A call for passive resistance went out, namely in the form of boycotts of the census being organized by the Polish authori ties, conscription into the army, and elections to the Sejm (November 1922). In October 1919 circles of underground Ukrainian education began forming, and July 1921 an underground university (existing until 1925) opened its doors.
texts.8: The transfer of farms to Polish colonists was particularly resented – local peas ants commonly believed that the colonists appropriated land that should belong to them instead. The Ukrainians by no means intended to limit themselves to passive resis tance. Some Ukrainian officers and soldiers refused to lay down arms. In the summer of 1920, the underground Ukrainian Military Organization (UVO) was formed, headed by Colonel Yevhen Konovalets. The name of the organization rather inadvertently alluded to the Polish Military Organization ( bers of the UVO would later use Polish experiences in the struggle for inde pendence as a touchstone. Initially, UVO subordinated itself to Petrushevych’s government-in-exile in Vienna. Immediately after its creation, the organization began operations aimed at opposing the incorporation of Eastern Galicia and other disputed territories into the Republic of Poland. The first UVO terrorist act was carried out on November 25, 1921, in Lviv: an unsuccessful attempt on Marshal J zef Piłsudski’s life (with the accompanying Lviv Voivode Kazimierz Grabowski being wounded). Sabotage actions carried out under Konovalets’ direct leadership in the summer and autumn of 1922 were more serious. Grain stacks and farms of newly settled colonists and other Poles were set on fire. Bombs were planted at police and railroad stations, military warehouses, and on telegraph and telephone poles. Operations included the burning of mili tary warehouses near Przemyśl and police buildings in Yavoriv, Grdek, Uhniv and Lubacz w. As part of a liquidation of “traitors”, on October 15, 1922, in Kamianka Strumilova ( day UVO members killed Sydir Tverdohlib, a Ukrainian poet and journalist, leader of the Agrarian Ukrainian Peasants’ Party and candidate for the Polish Sejm. This sabotage campaign, supported by communist circles, lasted several months. Three hundred acts of sabotage and diversion were likely committed. Police statistics list 223 acts of sabotage in 1922, including 17 attacks on officials (with five killed), 15 attacks on Ukrainian conciliators (nine deaths), 129 acts of arson and robberies, 27 sabotages of state facilities, and 35 telephone and telegraph wire cutting incidents.
texts.9:
All this, however, failed to alter the Ukrainians’ position on the international stage. On March 14, 1923, the Council of Ambassadors, which had succeeded the Supreme War Council at the Paris Peace Conference, granted Eastern Galicia to Poland with the expectation that the local government of these ter ritories would be given certain autonomous rights. The decision of the Council of Ambassadors seemed to close the issue of Poland’s eastern border, at least in the perception of most western Ukrainians. This quickly eroded the authority of the Petrushevych government, with which even the UVO ceased coopera tion in its determination to continue its desperate struggle.

On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the  
Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lwów) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian  
flags  appeared  on  government  offices  and  announcements  circulated  the  
city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic (WUPR) had been  
established  with  Lviv  as  its  capital.  For  those  Leopolitans  who  dreamed  of  
a  free  Poland,  the  prospect  of  becoming West  Ukrainian  citizens  was  unac-  
ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a  
state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but  
was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and  
increased desires to actively oppose these developments.  
That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching  
counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into  
fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under  
seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting,  
giving rise to the legend of the Lwów Eaglets. On November 22, 1918 – due to  
resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left  
Lviv.  This  was,  however,  only  the  beginning  of  the  Polish-Ukrainian  war,  or  
rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war.  
By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu-  
vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units  
went on the offensive. Partial forces from General Józef Haller’s army, which  
had  arrived  from  France,  were  used  for  this  purpose  (though  promises  had  
been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in  
Galicia).  Polish  pressure  forced  the  bleeding WUPR  units  to  retreat  behind  
the  Zbruch  River,  which  was  to  form  the  southeastern  border  of  a  reborn

Poland. The  last  units  crossed  over  on  July  16,  1919. The WUPR government  
led by Yevhen Petrushevych went first to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and then into  
exile. The incorporation of the WUPR into the Polish Republic was accepted  
by the leader of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Symon Petliura, who wanted  
thereby  to  save  Ukrainian  statehood  on  the  Dnieper  River.  As  is  known,  his  
hopes were dashed by the unfolding of the Polish-Soviet War and the Peace of

Despite military defeat, western Ukrainians did not lose hope for indepen dence. The Poles had trouble getting the victorious powers, mainly France and England, to agree to Poland’s incorporation of Eastern Galicia. In June 1919 Poland was granted only the right of temporary administration over the region, while serious consideration was given to the idea that its fate should be decided by inhabitants themselves in a plebiscite held under the auspices of the League of Nations. Though Lviv was a Polish city, Ukrainians were the majority in the remainder of Eastern Galicia. According to the 1931 census, Lviv was inhabited by 157,000 Poles, 99,000 Jews, and just under 50,000 Ukrainians, yet of the 4,729,515 people living in all of Eastern Galicia, 2,847,844 were Greek Catholics (almost entirely Ukrainians), 1,350,978 declared themselves to be Roman Catholics (Poles), and 490,459 professed Judaism (Jews). The results of any plebiscite would have therefore certainly been unfavourable for Poland. The authorities of the Second Polish Republic, realizing this danger, began to strengthen Polish identity in the Kresy (Polish for “borderlands”) imme diately following the victory. Government offices were first to be Polonized, with all individuals refusing to swear an oath of allegiance to the Polish state being removed. Next, the Ukrainian chairs at the University of Lviv were abol ished and a principle by which only those Polish citizens who had served in the Polish Army could study there was adopted. Finally, on December 5, 1920, all of Galicia was divided into four voivodeships (provinces): Krak w, Lw w,
The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic

Tarnopol, and Stanisł w. The borders of these provinces were shifted west ward to change their demographic composition in favour of the Polish popula tion. Thus, Lw w Voivodeship came to include powiats (counties) inhabited mainly by Poles: Rzesz w, Kolbuszowa, Krosno, and Tarnobrzeg. Eastern Galicia was officially named Eastern Lesser Poland (Wschodnia Małopolska Moreover, in December 1920 the Legislative Sejm (Poland’s parliament) passed a law that granted farmsteads in Volhynia on favourable financial terms to deserving soldiers and war invalids from central Poland, who were often set tled in isolated settlements. These actions provoked opposition from a large portion of the Ukrainian population. The Ukrainian political parties did not recognize Polish statehood, accepting only the exiled government as a legal authority. A similar position was taken, among others, by the leader of the Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytskyi. A call for passive resistance went out, namely in the form of boycotts of the census being organized by the Polish authori ties, conscription into the army, and elections to the Sejm (November 1922). In October 1919 circles of underground Ukrainian education began forming, and July 1921 an underground university (existing until 1925) opened its doors.

The transfer of farms to Polish colonists was particularly resented – local peas ants commonly believed that the colonists appropriated land that should belong to them instead. The Ukrainians by no means intended to limit themselves to passive resis tance. Some Ukrainian officers and soldiers refused to lay down arms. In the summer of 1920, the underground Ukrainian Military Organization (UVO) was formed, headed by Colonel Yevhen Konovalets. The name of the organization rather inadvertently alluded to the Polish Military Organization ( bers of the UVO would later use Polish experiences in the struggle for inde pendence as a touchstone. Initially, UVO subordinated itself to Petrushevych’s government-in-exile in Vienna. Immediately after its creation, the organization began operations aimed at opposing the incorporation of Eastern Galicia and other disputed territories into the Republic of Poland. The first UVO terrorist act was carried out on November 25, 1921, in Lviv: an unsuccessful attempt on Marshal J zef Piłsudski’s life (with the accompanying Lviv Voivode Kazimierz Grabowski being wounded). Sabotage actions carried out under Konovalets’ direct leadership in the summer and autumn of 1922 were more serious. Grain stacks and farms of newly settled colonists and other Poles were set on fire. Bombs were planted at police and railroad stations, military warehouses, and on telegraph and telephone poles. Operations included the burning of mili tary warehouses near Przemyśl and police buildings in Yavoriv, Grdek, Uhniv and Lubacz w. As part of a liquidation of “traitors”, on October 15, 1922, in Kamianka Strumilova ( day UVO members killed Sydir Tverdohlib, a Ukrainian poet and journalist, leader of the Agrarian Ukrainian Peasants’ Party and candidate for the Polish Sejm. This sabotage campaign, supported by communist circles, lasted several months. Three hundred acts of sabotage and diversion were likely committed. Police statistics list 223 acts of sabotage in 1922, including 17 attacks on officials (with five killed), 15 attacks on Ukrainian conciliators (nine deaths), 129 acts of arson and robberies, 27 sabotages of state facilities, and 35 telephone and telegraph wire cutting incidents.

All this, however, failed to alter the Ukrainians’ position on the international stage. On March 14, 1923, the Council of Ambassadors, which had succeeded the Supreme War Council at the Paris Peace Conference, granted Eastern Galicia to Poland with the expectation that the local government of these ter ritories would be given certain autonomous rights. The decision of the Council of Ambassadors seemed to close the issue of Poland’s eastern border, at least in the perception of most western Ukrainians. This quickly eroded the authority of the Petrushevych government, with which even the UVO ceased coopera tion in its determination to continue its desperate struggle.

On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the  
Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lwów) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian  
flags  appeared  on  government  offices  and  announcements  circulated  the  
city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic (WUPR) had been  
established  with  Lviv  as  its  capital.  For  those  Leopolitans  who  dreamed  of  
a  free  Poland,  the  prospect  of  becoming West  Ukrainian  citizens  was  unac-  
ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a  
state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but  
was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and  
increased desires to actively oppose these developments.  
That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching  
counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into  
fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under  
seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting,  
giving rise to the legend of the Lwów Eaglets. On November 22, 1918 – due to  
resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left  
Lviv.  This  was,  however,  only  the  beginning  of  the  Polish-Ukrainian  war,  or  
rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war.  
By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu-  
vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units  
went on the offensive. Partial forces from General Józef Haller’s army, which  
had  arrived  from  France,  were  used  for  this  purpose  (though  promises  had  
been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in  
Galicia).  Polish  pressure  forced  the  bleeding WUPR  units  to  retreat  behind  
the  Zbruch  River,  which  was  to  form  the  southeastern  border  of  a  reborn  

## [PDF page 12]
Poland. The  last  units  crossed  over  on  July  16,  1919. The WUPR government  
led by Yevhen Petrushevych went first to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and then into  
exile. The incorporation of the WUPR into the Polish Republic was accepted  
by the leader of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Symon Petliura, who wanted  
thereby  to  save  Ukrainian  statehood  on  the  Dnieper  River.  As  is  known,  his  
hopes were dashed by the unfolding of the Polish-Soviet War and the Peace of  
Riga signed in March 1921.

Participation  in  the  meetings  of  the  PVC  or  the  Delegation  (of  the  Sejm)  caused  
S. Stempowski irritation and disagreement with the majority of the decisions made. Thus,  
he added his separate opinion to the Memorial to the Chairman of the Council of Ministers  
Ignacy  Paderewski  from  the  PVC.  In  it,  S.  Stempowski  opposed  the  main  provisions  of  
the  document,  in  particular  the  annexation  of  Right-Bank  Ukraine  to  Poland,  which  was  
in fact “a call for a war of annexation in the region where the Poles make up only a small  
percentage, and which will cause the Ukrainian people to reject the Poles and Poland forever”  
(Stempowski, 1972, p.  69). He argued that the Ukrainian people were incapable of statehood.  
Later, S. Stempowski opposed the participation of the Central Committee representatives in  
the meetings of the PVC, believing that the PVC participation and silent opposition gave the  
Edeks advantages and triumphs through joint decisions (Stempowski, 1972, p. 73).  
S. Petliura initiated the sending of a special UNR mission to Warsaw on December 31,  
1918, headed by Viacheslav Prokopovych. The UNR mission was to clarify the conditions  
for reaching an agreement on joint actions against Bolshevik Russia and receiving assistance  
(S. Stempowski participated in meetings held in Jewhen Starczewski's house and conferences  
initiated by him with the Ukrainians from the embassy, in particular the ambassador Leonid  
Mykhailiv,  the  advisors  Prokop  Poniatenko  and  Borys  Repetsky).  S.  Stempowski  was  
interested in the Ukrainian issue and events in Ukraine everywhere. In September of 1919,  

## [PDF page 9]
Jewhen Starczewski managed to visit Podillia as a journalist together with the Polish trade  
mission led by Józef Lipkowski and several government officials from various ministries.  
During  the  trip,  he  noted  a  significant  number  of  soldiers,  the  Ukrainian  language  in  the  
streets  of  Kamianets,  and  the  Ukrainian  army,  which  lacked  weapons,  ammunition,  and  
clothing (Stempowski, 1972, p. 84).  
In Warsaw Henryk Józewski was one of S. Stempowski's closest friends, who arrived  
in Warsaw in January of 1919. From the first meeting until the end of his life, they walked  
together. Henryk Józewski considered his older comrade a father, owing to whom he got to  
know the intellectual world of Warsaw and met prominent and well-known people. Later  
Henryk Józewski recalled that “we were together at all moments of the formation of Poland  
and the liberation struggle for Ukraine” (Józewski, 1982a, p. 46).  
Soon, through the mediation of a representative of the Democratic Central, S.  Stempowski  
became  the  head  of  the  press  department  in  the  Civil Administration  of  the  Volyn  and  
Podillia Front, whose chief commissar was former Minister Antoniy Minkiewicz. During  
his tours in the Volyn Voivodeship, S. Stempowski noticed that the pro-ENDEK officers and  
civil administration held fast to nationalist concepts and were convinced that it was possible  
and  necessary  to  resolve  all  national  and  religious  issues  by  armed  force  (Stempowski,  
1972, p. 85).  
In January of 1920, Stanisław Stempowski visited Ukraine as an advisor to the Minister  
in the government of the Volyn Land and the Podillia Front. After an understanding between  
Józef  Piłsudski  and  Symon  Petliura  for  the  better  implementation  of  the  Warsaw  Pact,

ideas and advocated granting the Polish minority national and cultural autonomy within  
the UNR.  
There  is  not  much  information  on  S.  Stempowski's  affiliation  with  Freemasonry.  It  is  
known that at the end of 1920, some personalities among the Ukrainian community formed  
the Ukrainian Masonic lodge “Unity” in Poland, which became part of the recently founded  
Grand Lodge “United Poles” (Polacy Zjednoczeni – in Polish). It is assumed that one of the  
leaders of the new lodge was Stanisław Stempowski, a member of the Central Ukrainian  
Committee, an institution that emerged after the liquidation of the Ukrainian government.  
Perhaps this lodge included other Poles from Ukraine, supporters of the Polish-Ukrainian  
understanding  and  federalism.  It  is  also  known  that  Stanisław  Stempowski's  son  Jerzy  
considered the possibility of publishing his father's memoirs owing to the Grand Master of  
the US Lodge, who visited Poland and knew him well. Based on the Decree of the President  
of Poland of November 22, 1938 on the liquidation of Masonic lodges, they were “considered  
liquidated by virtue of the law itself”. On October 26, 1939, the Grand Lodge of Poland  
announced its self-liquidation. At the same time, as Jerzy Stempowski recalls, on the orders  
of  the  Minister  of  the  Internal Affairs  Felicien  Sławo-Składowski,  the  police  carried  out  
several “barbaric” searches in S.  Stempowski’s house” (Listy, 1991, p. 18). The fact that  
S. Stempowski belonged to Freemasonry was also recorded in the Gestapo report in Warsaw

_"War is to man what motherhood is to a woman. From a philosophical and doctrinal viewpoint, I do not believe in perpetual peace."_**- Benito Mussolini**​
Before the Cripps Memorandum leaked to the British press, the initial reactions within the British Foreign Office suggested that its content largely aligned with the instructions given to the ambassador, and the few noted discrepancies were initially considered minor. For example, in a comment dated October 24, Laurence Collier, head of the FO’s Northern Department, acknowledged that Cripps’s use of the term "de facto sovereignty" - implying more than mere "de facto control" - might raise objections from the Polish government. However, he completely overlooked the fact that the British ambassador had referred in the memorandum to the "former Polish state." Such terminology was not only contrary to international law, but also to the official guidelines of British foreign policy. Only later was Collier alerted to Cripps’s use of the phrase "former Polish state," yet even then he naively assumed the wording was simply the result of careless drafting rather than a reflection of Cripps’s political views. He also failed to recognize the significance such a phrase might hold for the Soviet side and how difficult it would be to walk it back — not just in terms of changing the language, but in terms of reversing the implicit territorial concessions. Ultimately, the Foreign Office decided that a retraction attempt had to be made. On October 30, in a cable to Cripps, Halifax, in very mild language, urged the ambassador to try to retract the terms “sovereignty” and “former,” while adding that “in a case of absolute necessity, we may have to accept ‘sovereignty,’ but in light of our relationship and agreements with Poland we cannot speak of the ‘former Polish state’ in an international arrangement.” Cripps’s response made it clear that (contrary to Collier’s belief) his wording was no accident or oversight but rather reflected his political stance at the time. Justifying his use of “de facto sovereignty,” Cripps pointed out that he had already employed the term in proposals submitted to the Foreign Office on October 13, which had not been contested.

He further argued that “in the Russian translation given to Vyshinsky, a somewhat vague word vlast’, meaning ‘authority’ or ‘dominion,’ was used, and that it would not be difficult to explain to the Soviet government that it was intended as a rendering of the English term control, which lacks an exact equivalent in Russian.” As for using the phrase “former Polish state,” His Majesty’s ambassador stated: “I was not aware that His Majesty’s Government wished to maintain the fiction that the former Polish state, as distinct from the government, still de facto existed anywhere outside of African Togoland"[1]. While the British were still deliberating internally on the final wording of the prospective Anglo-Soviet agreement, the Bolsheviks struck a deal with the Third Reich on the division of spheres of influence in Romania and concluded a new Soviet-German trade agreement. Then came November. On November 8, 1940, a joint Afghan-German invasion of British India began. Both pieces of news stunned London.

The day after the German-Afghan attack on British India, on November 9 an urgent meeting took place between Molotov and Cripps[2]. Taking advantage of the international situation, Molotov spoke to Cripps from a position of strength. The Soviet side informed the British that the USSR intended to remain neutral in the German-British conflict, while at the same time maintaining its trade agreement with the Third Reich. Molotov emphasized that the Soviet Union was open to discussing a non-aggression pact with the United Kingdom, in exchange for full recognition of the USSR's new borders in Europe and Asia, recognition of the new communist governments in Romania and Bulgaria, and the prevention of attacks on Soviet ships in the Atlantic by Italian and French forces. The Soviet demands were soon reinforced by a special address delivered the next day by Joseph Stalin, in which he referred to the German attack on British India and underscored Soviet neutrality. In his speech, Stalin described the Soviet Union as a “state of peace” that was at war only with Japan, though still open to a peaceful resolution of that conflict. His statement made no mention of the ongoing state of war between the USSR and Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, Austria-Hungary, Spain, and France. Stalin also declared his readiness to host potential peace talks between Germany and Britain if both sides agree to such negotiations. Molotov’s demands and Stalin’s address sparked mixed reactions in London. On one hand, there was relief that the USSR did not plan to join the attack on India, which was welcomed by left-wing circles in the British government as a major success of Cripps's mission. On the other hand, it was recognized that the USSR continued to view the Third Reich as its principal partner, and that the Soviet demands concerning the terms of a non-aggression treaty were excessively high. Before the British could issue a formal response, on November 16, information about the British-Soviet negotiations and the British proposals to Moscow leaked to the press. On November 18, The Times published a detailed article on the subject. Making such details public inevitably provoked strong reactions. According to the minutes from the War Cabinet meeting held on the same day, it was not expected that the revelations would significantly affect Soviet policy, and no mention was made of anticipated reactions from Italy, France, Japan, or especially Poland. However, the Axis governments’ response was immediate and unequivocal.

Before examining the steps they took, it must be emphasized that Italian, French, Japanese, and Polish politicians were completely taken aback by the information that had reached the press. These governments had neither been informed nor, even less, consulted by their British ally during negotiations with the Soviet government. Although the Axis powers were aware that Cripps had been conducting talks in Moscow “on trade matters and beyond,” and that Britain was not inclined to go to war with the USSR despite Mussolini’s requests, no one suspected the scope of those discussions. An example of this overly optimistic assessment can be seen in a memorandum written by the Polish ambassador to London, Edward Raczyński, to Foreign Minister August Zaleski on November 11. Raczyński wrote: “Prime Minister Churchill holds the view that Soviet aid to England is only possible in two scenarios: (1) if the Soviets become convinced that the Third Reich has already lost the war; (2) if the Soviets themselves feel directly threatened. In neither case is there any justification for paying off the Soviets in exchange for assistance. Hence the conclusion and, for now, the certainty that Great Britain has not made the Soviets any promises at our expense, even unofficially, nor does it intend to do so"[3].

Given assessments like that of Ambassador Raczyński, it is hardly surprising that the Polish government—and the rest of the Axis Powers—reacted with outrage to the press reports about British proposals toward Moscow. Although Molotov's demands had not leaked, the content of Cripps’s memorandum alone came as a huge shock. As a result, on November 18, Zaleski flew from Rome to London to meet with Halifax. During the meeting, held that afternoon, the Polish Foreign Minister protested against the British government making any commitments to the USSR without consulting its Polish ally. He emphasized that Poland was at war with the Soviet Union and that, for this reason alone, the Polish government should be consulted on whether the USSR should be allowed to participate in future peace negotiations. In response to Zaleski’s questions and objections, Halifax confirmed that His Majesty’s Government had made “certain proposals” to the Soviet government in an attempt to persuade it to abandon its pro-German policy. However, he insisted that the British held “no illusions” about Soviet policy and had been “especially cautious” when discussing matters in Moscow that might affect Polish interests. Halifax concluded by assuring Zaleski that the proposals presented to the Soviet government envisioned only a “temporary arrangement based on the existing state of affairs, which we can neither deny nor ignore.” This response, however, was unsatisfactory to the Poles. In response to the Polish-British crisis in relations, Poland received strong support from Mussolini. The Italian Duce, following talks with Polish Prime Minister General Sikorski and viewing himself as the leader of the anti-communist camp, reacted immediately by convening a special conference of Axis leaders or ambassadors in Naples on November 22. The conference was attended by official representatives of nine powers: Italy, France, Japan, Poland, Austria-Hungary, Spain, Bulgaria, Thailand, and Belgium. Additionally, representatives of several quasi-state entities were present, including the Empire of Vietnam and the Maronite Lebanese Phalange, which controlled the County of Tripoli in Lebanon (both previously mentioned are part of French Colonial Empire); the Kingdom of Albania and the Kingdom of Illyria (states in personal union with Italy); the Russian Empire and the Chinese Empire (both under Japanese influence); the Free City of Danzig (a Polish-dependent entity); and the commander-in-chief of the Jewish forces in Italy - Polish-born Jewish fascist Avraham Stern, who took leadership after the death of Ze’ev Jabotinsky.

As a result of the conference, the representatives of the aforementioned states and entities signed the so-called “Neapolitan Pact,” also referred to as the “Axis Pact.” In the preamble to the document, the signatories blamed liberal democracy for the outbreak of world war II, not only for bringing Hitler to power in Germany but also, according to the text, for triggering the Spanish Civil War, weakening France, and causing its defeats in May and June of 1940. The Neapolitan Pact explicitly imposed an obligation on its signatories to support a new postwar vision of the world, in which liberal democracy would be replaced by a corporatist system based on a strong monarchy and the defense of religious values.
In its first article, drafted in direct reaction to the British-Soviet talks, the Axis Pact obligated all signatories to undertake military actions against the Third Reich, the Republic of China, and the Soviet Union until those states were destroyed.
According to the second article, the signatories of the Axis Pact recognized the Russian Empire, ruled by Tsar Vladimir Kirillovich Romanov, as the sole lawful and legitimate Russian state. The Tsar was acknowledged to have rightful authority over the territories of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and other regions of the Soviet Union, with due consideration given to the principle of self-determination for various nations (particularly those that had sovereign states in 1920) as well as to Japan’s legitimate interests in the Far East and Poland’s in Eastern Europe.
The third article recognized the Chinese Empire under Emperor Xuantong (Aisin Gioro Puyi) as the sole legitimate Chinese state. However, it specified that, after the war, its borders should be limited to the ethnic Chinese heartland, excluding Manchuria, Mongolia, Turkestan, Tibet, Yunnan, and Canton.
The fourth article stated that the unification of Germany in 1871 was an illegal act and that one of the goals of the war should be the re-division of Germany into independent states such as Bavaria, Württemberg, Saxony, Hanover, Baden, Hesse, Prussia, and Mecklenburg, which would never be allowed to reunite.

The fifth article proposed the creation of State of the Church in the Holy Land, encompassing Jerusalem and Bethlehem, surrounded by an independent Jewish state, which, as described, would include the entire area of the British Mandate of Palestine, excluding the aforementioned Christian State.
The subsequent articles of the Axis Pact, which dealt with border issues in Europe and Asia, were classified and withheld from public disclosure. The agreements made in this section of the pact essentially formalized numerous informal arrangements that the leaders of the signatory states had established among themselves over the preceding months of the war.
Regarding Italy, the pact stipulated that Italy was entitled to annex the southwestern regions of Anatolia according to the boundaries outlined in the Treaty of London, the Greek Ionian Islands (which had been under de facto Italian occupation since 1939), the Spanish Balearic Islands (under de facto Italian occupation since 1937)[4], as well as all Croatian, Slovenian, and Albanian territories within Yugoslavia. These territories were to form the Kingdoms of Illyria and Albania, united in a personal union with Italy. The core Serbian and Montenegrin lands were to form a reconstituted Kingdom of Serbia, a protectorate under Italian rule, governed by the Montenegrin Petrović-Njegoš dynasty[5]. Furthermore, Italian forces were to regain the perpetual right to be stationed within Austria-Hungary.
With regard to Spain, it was agreed that the pact's signatories supported the idea of unifying Spain with Portugal, should the populations of both countries express such a will[6]. The pact also recognized Spanish-Portuguese claims to Indonesian islands inhabited predominantly by Christians, the Iranian coastline, and the city of Tangier, which was to pass from its Franco-Spanish condominium status to full Spanish control, in exchange for transferring Andorra to full French sovereignty.
In the case of France, the pact acknowledged French claims to the former Saar Protectorate and surrounding Rhineland territories, emphasizing that the natural Franco-German border should be defined by the Moselle and Rhine rivers. The remaining portion of the Rhineland was to be granted to Luxembourg. Regarding French colonies, it was agreed that in exchange for France relinquishing Cambodia and Laos to Thailand, all of Southeast China including Yunnan and the expanded Greater Canton region would become a French protectorate. The Empire of Vietnam and the County of Tripoli were to gain a special status within the French Colonial Empire.

Regarding Austria-Hungary, it was agreed that the ruler of Austria-Hungary would hold primacy among Catholic German monarchs. Austrian claims to the southern and western parts of Bohemia, and Hungarian claims to Bačka, Baranja, Medimurje, Prekmurje, Banat, northen Transylvania, southern and eastern Slovakia, and Transcarpathia, were recognized[7].
As for Poland, it was agreed that its borders would be expanded at the expense of Germany to include all of East Prussia, Frontier March of Posen–West Prussia, Breslau, and all of Silesia up to the Oder River, as well as the cities of Słupsk and Kolberg in Pomerania; at the expense of Czechoslovakia to include Cieszyn Silesia, Spisz, and Orava; and at the expense of the USSR to include Minsk, Zhytomyr, and Kamianets-Podilskyi. Poland, as a monarchy, was also to reunite with Lithuania into a restored Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth[8].
In the case of Bulgaria, the pact recognized Bulgarian claims to Romanian Dobrudja, Greek and Turkish Thrace including the city of Constantinople, and Yugoslav territories inhabited by Bulgarians (including Macedonians).
Regarding Belgium, it was agreed that the residents of the Walloon territories, which had been removed from Belgium by Hitler and incorporated into the puppet French State, would be allowed to determine their own state affiliation through a plebiscite. In exchange for agreeing to this plebiscite, Belgium would gain, at the expense of the Netherlands, the regions of North Brabant, Dutch Limburg, and Zeelandic Flanders, and at the expense of Germany, the city of Aachen on the Belgian-German border.
Concerning Japan, the pact recognized Japanese authority over Sakhalin, Hainan Island, all of Manchuria (which was to become an autonomous province within Japan after the war) and the Chinese Shandong Peninsula. Furthermore, Japanese influence over the Chinese Empire, the proposed Mongolian State, and an independent Muslim Indonesia was acknowledged.

Only some of the proposals included in the Neapolitan Pact were actually implemented after the end of World War II. The contents of the Neapolitan Pact were communicated to the ambassadors of the allied countries - Portugal, Brazil, Greece, and the United Kingdom- yet none of them signed this Pact, resulting in Portugal and Brazil no longer being recognized as Axis Powers. Mussolini, above all, sought to provoke a reaction from the United Kingdom, demanding that the British ambassador to Italy, James Eric Drummond, ensure that Britain joined the pact and ceased negotiations with the Soviet Union. For Mussolini, this was a matter of great importance, as several thousand Italian soldiers were imprisoned in Soviet camps and prisons. In response to this crisis, Winston Churchill undertook a week-long visit to Italy in the second half of November. During this visit, he was forced to negotiate and explain recent media reports to representatives of the Axis Powers, in particular Benito Mussolini, Galeazzo Ciano, and the Polish Prime Minister, General Władysław Sikorski. Sikorski emphasized to Churchill that the actions of Cripps could not serve as a precedent on which the Soviets might base their arguments concerning Poland’s eastern borders. To repair relations, Churchill stressed that the United Kingdom did not intend to support the seizure of Polish territory. He proposed that Britain could support Polish claims to Lithuania, East Prussia, and Upper Silesia and offered guarantees that, after the end of World War II, Poland's territory would not be smaller than it was in 1939. This guarantee laid the foundation for the Roman Charter, signed at the end of November. The charter stated that none of the countries belonging to the Anti-Hitler Coalition would be territorially diminished after the war. The Roman Charter was signed by both the signatories of the Axis Pact and by the United Kingdom as well as all other nations fighting against Germany. The text of the Roman Charter marked the first historical use of the term "Anti-Hitler Coalition" - a compromise between Mussolini, who disliked the term “Allies” due to its associations with World War I and what he considered a “mutilated victory,” and Churchill, who refused to refer to Britain as an Axis Power. Churchill’s private conversation with Mussolini proved far more difficult than his discussion with Sikorski. In response to Mussolini’s accusations of British betrayal, Churchill brought up Italy’s concealment of cryptographic technology related to breaking the German Enigma code, something British intelligence had discovered.

The dispute between Mussolini and Churchill was eventually defused by Galeazzo Ciano, who proposed that in exchange for shared cryptographic technology across the Anti-Hitler Coalition, Italy (and France) would be granted co-control of the Suez Canal. Additionally, Italian forces in Libya and Abyssinia, along with the Jewish Legion based in Italy, would join the campaign in the Middle East. Churchill ultimately agreed to Ciano’s proposal, recognizing that after the Afghan attack on India, British forces were overstretched and in need of assistance in the occupation of Egypt and military operations across the Middle East - especially as the Egyptian King Farouk I’s inner circle was openly pro-German, posing a real threat of Egypt joining the Vampire Bloc.​
[1] Except for the reference to Togo, the entire content is a fragment of OTL described in the article titled "The Stafford Cripps Memorandum of October 22, 1940: Polish Aspects" by Magdalena Hułas.
[2] In OTL, Molotov refused all proposals for a meeting with Cripps for quite some time, but in this ATL, I assumed that in the context of a German-Afghan attack on British India, Molotov could not reject Cripps.
[3] The text of Ambassador Raczyński’s note comes from OTL.
[4] In OTL, the Italians attempted to take the Balearic Islands from the Spanish as compensation for Italian support of General Franco. During the occupation of the islands, the Italians tried to Italianize them.
[5] Of course, this is a dynasty closely intermarried with the royal family ruling in Italy.
[6] For General Franco, the idea of unifying Portugal with Spain was a key objective in the 1940s.
[7] I assume that Mussolini did not want the Austro-Hungarian Empire to become too large territorially, fearing it might gain independence from Italy in the future.

[8] Interestingly, concepts for rebuilding the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth also appeared in Polish visions during WWII in OTL. General Sikorski's OTL ideas envisioned a federation combining Poland, Czechoslovakia, and sometimes Lithuania into a single monarchic state. Another concept in OTL was developed in the early days of September 1939 during the border battles and after France and the UK had declared war on Germany. At that time, a veterans’ organization in Lwów managed to draft the first territorial demands for the Second Polish Republic following a victorious war (see map below). Fascinatingly, this map was circulated before the Germans reached Lwów, with a fairly large print run—into the four digits. The map illustrated Poland’s most radical claims against Germany at the time, while preserving the eastern borders of the Second Republic. It even went a step further by incorporating the entire Republic of Lithuania into future Poland, justified by the vision of a "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth." It was the story of this map that inspired me to present Poland's claims in this way.

The Tsar was acknowledged to have rightful authority over the territories of the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic and other regions of the Soviet Union, with due consideration given to the principle of self-determination for various nations (particularly those that had sovereign states in 1920) as well as to Japan’s legitimate interests in the Far East and Poland’s in Eastern Europe.
The third article recognized the Chinese Empire under Emperor Xuantong (Aisin Gioro Puyi) as the sole legitimate Chinese state. However, it specified that, after the war, its borders should be limited to the ethnic Chinese heartland, excluding Manchuria, Mongolia, Turkestan, Tibet, Yunnan, and Canton.
The fourth article stated that the unification of Germany in 1871 was an illegal act and that one of the goals of the war should be the re-division of Germany into independent states such as Bavaria, Württemberg, Saxony, Hanover, Baden, Hesse, Prussia, and Mecklenburg, which would never be allowed to reunite.
texts.6:
The fifth article proposed the creation of State of the Church in the Holy Land, encompassing Jerusalem and Bethlehem, surrounded by an independent Jewish state, which, as described, would include the entire area of the British Mandate of Palestine, excluding the aforementioned Christian State.
The subsequent articles of the Axis Pact, which dealt with border issues in Europe and Asia, were classified and withheld from public disclosure. The agreements made in this section of the pact essentially formalized numerous informal arrangements that the leaders of the signatory states had established among themselves over the preceding months of the war.
Regarding Italy, the pact stipulated that Italy was entitled to annex the southwestern regions of Anatolia according to the boundaries outlined in the Treaty of London, the Greek Ionian Islands (which had been under de facto Italian occupation since 1939), the Spanish Balearic Islands (under de facto Italian occupation since 1937)[4], as well as all Croatian, Slovenian, and Albanian territories within Yugoslavia. These territories were to form the Kingdoms of Illyria and Albania, united in a personal union with Italy. The core Serbian and Montenegrin lands were to form a reconstituted Kingdom of Serbia, a protectorate under Italian rule, governed by the Montenegrin Petrović-Njegoš dynasty[5]. Furthermore, Italian forces were to regain the perpetual right to be stationed within Austria-Hungary.
With regard to Spain, it was agreed that the pact's signatories supported the idea of unifying Spain with Portugal, should the populations of both countries express such a will[6]. The pact also recognized Spanish-Portuguese claims to Indonesian islands inhabited predominantly by Christians, the Iranian coastline, and the city of Tangier, which was to pass from its Franco-Spanish condominium status to full Spanish control, in exchange for transferring Andorra to full French sovereignty.
In the case of France, the pact acknowledged French claims to the former Saar Protectorate and surrounding Rhineland territories, emphasizing that the natural Franco-German border should be defined by the Moselle and Rhine rivers. The remaining portion of the Rhineland was to be granted to Luxembourg. Regarding French colonies, it was agreed that in exchange for France relinquishing Cambodia and Laos to Thailand, all of Southeast China including Yunnan and the expanded Greater Canton region would become a French protectorate. The Empire of Vietnam and the County of Tripoli were to gain a special status within the French Colonial Empire.
texts.7:
Regarding Austria-Hungary, it was agreed that the ruler of Austria-Hungary would hold primacy among Catholic German monarchs. Austrian claims to the southern and western parts of Bohemia, and Hungarian claims to Bačka, Baranja, Medimurje, Prekmurje, Banat, northen Transylvania, southern and eastern Slovakia, and Transcarpathia, were recognized[7].
As for Poland, it was agreed that its borders would be expanded at the expense of Germany to include all of East Prussia, Frontier March of Posen–West Prussia, Breslau, and all of Silesia up to the Oder River, as well as the cities of Słupsk and Kolberg in Pomerania; at the expense of Czechoslovakia to include Cieszyn Silesia, Spisz, and Orava; and at the expense of the USSR to include Minsk, Zhytomyr, and Kamianets-Podilskyi. Poland, as a monarchy, was also to reunite with Lithuania into a restored Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth[8].
In the case of Bulgaria, the pact recognized Bulgarian claims to Romanian Dobrudja, Greek and Turkish Thrace including the city of Constantinople, and Yugoslav territories inhabited by Bulgarians (including Macedonians).
Regarding Belgium, it was agreed that the residents of the Walloon territories, which had been removed from Belgium by Hitler and incorporated into the puppet French State, would be allowed to determine their own state affiliation through a plebiscite. In exchange for agreeing to this plebiscite, Belgium would gain, at the expense of the Netherlands, the regions of North Brabant, Dutch Limburg, and Zeelandic Flanders, and at the expense of Germany, the city of Aachen on the Belgian-German border.
Concerning Japan, the pact recognized Japanese authority over Sakhalin, Hainan Island, all of Manchuria (which was to become an autonomous province within Japan after the war) and the Chinese Shandong Peninsula. Furthermore, Japanese influence over the Chinese Empire, the proposed Mongolian State, and an independent Muslim Indonesia was acknowledged.
texts.8: Only some of the proposals included in the Neapolitan Pact were actually implemented after the end of World War II. The contents of the Neapolitan Pact were communicated to the ambassadors of the allied countries - Portugal, Brazil, Greece, and the United Kingdom- yet none of them signed this Pact, resulting in Portugal and Brazil no longer being recognized as Axis Powers. Mussolini, above all, sought to provoke a reaction from the United Kingdom, demanding that the British ambassador to Italy, James Eric Drummond, ensure that Britain joined the pact and ceased negotiations with the Soviet Union. For Mussolini, this was a matter of great importance, as several thousand Italian soldiers were imprisoned in Soviet camps and prisons. In response to this crisis, Winston Churchill undertook a week-long visit to Italy in the second half of November. During this visit, he was forced to negotiate and explain recent media reports to representatives of the Axis Powers, in particular Benito Mussolini, Galeazzo Ciano, and the Polish Prime Minister, General Władysław Sikorski. Sikorski emphasized to Churchill that the actions of Cripps could not serve as a precedent on which the Soviets might base their arguments concerning Poland’s eastern borders. To repair relations, Churchill stressed that the United Kingdom did not intend to support the seizure of Polish territory. He proposed that Britain could support Polish claims to Lithuania, East Prussia, and Upper Silesia and offered guarantees that, after the end of World War II, Poland's territory would not be smaller than it was in 1939. This guarantee laid the foundation for the Roman Charter, signed at the end of November. The charter stated that none of the countries belonging to the Anti-Hitler Coalition would be territorially diminished after the war. The Roman Charter was signed by both the signatories of the Axis Pact and by the United Kingdom as well as all other nations fighting against Germany. The text of the Roman Charter marked the first historical use of the term "Anti-Hitler Coalition" - a compromise between Mussolini, who disliked the term “Allies” due to its associations with World War I and what he considered a “mutilated victory,” and Churchill, who refused to refer to Britain as an Axis Power. Churchill’s private conversation with Mussolini proved far more difficult than his discussion with Sikorski. In response to Mussolini’s accusations of British betrayal, Churchill brought up Italy’s concealment of cryptographic technology related to breaking the German Enigma code, something British intelligence had discovered.
texts.9:
The dispute between Mussolini and Churchill was eventually defused by Galeazzo Ciano, who proposed that in exchange for shared cryptographic technology across the Anti-Hitler Coalition, Italy (and France) would be granted co-control of the Suez Canal. Additionally, Italian forces in Libya and Abyssinia, along with the Jewish Legion based in Italy, would join the campaign in the Middle East. Churchill ultimately agreed to Ciano’s proposal, recognizing that after the Afghan attack on India, British forces were overstretched and in need of assistance in the occupation of Egypt and military operations across the Middle East - especially as the Egyptian King Farouk I’s inner circle was openly pro-German, posing a real threat of Egypt joining the Vampire Bloc.​
[1] Except for the reference to Togo, the entire content is a fragment of OTL described in the article titled "The Stafford Cripps Memorandum of October 22, 1940: Polish Aspects" by Magdalena Hułas.
[2] In OTL, Molotov refused all proposals for a meeting with Cripps for quite some time, but in this ATL, I assumed that in the context of a German-Afghan attack on British India, Molotov could not reject Cripps.
[3] The text of Ambassador Raczyński’s note comes from OTL.
[4] In OTL, the Italians attempted to take the Balearic Islands from the Spanish as compensation for Italian support of General Franco. During the occupation of the islands, the Italians tried to Italianize them.
[5] Of course, this is a dynasty closely intermarried with the royal family ruling in Italy.
[6] For General Franco, the idea of unifying Portugal with Spain was a key objective in the 1940s.
[7] I assume that Mussolini did not want the Austro-Hungarian Empire to become too large territorially, fearing it might gain independence from Italy in the future.
texts.10: [8] Interestingly, concepts for rebuilding the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth also appeared in Polish visions during WWII in OTL. General Sikorski's OTL ideas envisioned a federation combining Poland, Czechoslovakia, and sometimes Lithuania into a single monarchic state. Another concept in OTL was developed in the early days of September 1939 during the border battles and after France and the UK had declared war on Germany. At that time, a veterans’ organization in Lwów managed to draft the first territorial demands for the Second Polish Republic following a victorious war (see map below). Fascinatingly, this map was circulated before the Germans reached Lwów, with a fairly large print run—into the four digits. The map illustrated Poland’s most radical claims against Germany at the time, while preserving the eastern borders of the Second Republic. It even went a step further by incorporating the entire Republic of Lithuania into future Poland, justified by the vision of a "Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth." It was the story of this map that inspired me to present Poland's claims in this way.
