opened.information:
Source: https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/zelensky-says-u-raised-territory-143531181.html
Title: Zelensky says U.S. raised territory-for-NATO trade-off
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The United States has asked Ukraine whether it would withdraw troops from parts of the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, signaling a potential shift in President Donald Trump's previous opposition to Kyiv joining the Western military alliance.
Zelensky told reporters Friday that American negotiators raised the question for the first time, though he added that the discussions have not yielded a concrete proposal.
"The Americans asked: 'If Ukraine joins NATO, will Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" Zelensky said in remarks released Saturday.
The Ukrainian president stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian, while also rejecting the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution.
"If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway."
Russian President Vladimir Putin has long said NATO membership for Ukraine is a red line for his country, citing the issue as one reason for launching his invasion of Kyiv in February 2022.
Earlier this week, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials met in Abu Dhabi for their first trilateral negotiations in nine months. Meanwhile, European officials held separate talks with U.S. and Ukrainian counterparts there without engaging directly with Moscow.
The inquiry involves land in the Donbas that Ukrainian forces still control and Russian troops have failed to capture. Agreeing to pull back would force Ukrainians to weigh ceding territory their military has fought to defend against the promise of alliance protection from future Russian aggression.
_Newsweek_ has reached out to the State Department for comment.

## Shifting Messaging on NATO
The reported question marks a notable departure from Trump's earlier stance. In an August 2025 interview with Fox News, Trump ruled out Kyiv's entry into the alliance, saying, "They're not going to be a part of NATO." At the time, he suggested European nations should take the lead in defending Ukraine and ruled out deploying U.S. troops to protect its borders.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also downplayed the prospect of membership last month, citing the requirement for unanimous agreement among all NATO allies.
"Right now, we're simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict, if that's possible," Rubio said.
A joint statement on November 10 following talks among U.S., Ukrainian and European officials endorsed credible security guarantees for Kyiv and affirmed that "a strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defence," though it stopped short of backing Ukrainian membership. NATO maintains that Ukraine's future lies within the alliance, provided members agree and Kyiv meets necessary conditions.
U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff (right), Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speak to the media at the airport in Dublin on November 12. (AP Photo/Peter Morrison).

## Package of Guarantees
Zelensky said Kyiv is discussing a broader framework that includes security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, weapons and funding for Ukraine's military, and postwar reconstruction funds. Any formal proposal would have to be presented to the Ukrainian public, he said.
"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?" he said. "I have no right to make that decision on my own. But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet."
He reiterated that Kyiv will not recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied territory, meaning a troop withdrawal would leave Ukraine's claims to the land unresolved.
Zelensky also warned that Putin could use the negotiations to weaken NATO and redraw European borders, turning talks on ending the nearly five-year war into a wider bargain over continental security.
"Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."
Zelensky later added: "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."

## Europe Seeks a Seat at the Table
Addressing European leaders in Dublin on Thursday, Zelensky urged the bloc to secure a permanent role in the negotiations, characterizing U.S.-Russian discussions as "more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia."
Washington has acknowledged the talks carry wider implications. Jared Kushner, Trump's envoy and son-in-law, said European participation would allow negotiators to address "broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia."
Zelensky's remarks followed an agreement by EU leaders on Friday that Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland — known as the E5 — will represent Europe alongside EU institutions at the next round of peace talks, European Council President António Costa announced.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged allies on Friday to sustain pressure on the Kremlin.
"The best way to get Russia to the table is to keep up our support for Ukraine and to keep maximum pressure on Russia," she said.
The European Commission is preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia and a financing proposal for Ukraine ahead of a November 26–27 European Council summit.

Ahead of Friday's meeting, Trump repeated his long-standing claim that he would be able to "work out something" to settle the war if he won the presidential election, long before Joe Biden leaves office in January.
He has refused to elaborate when asked whether he believes Ukraine should cede territory to Russia as a means of ending the war.
Although Zelensky has been visiting the US since Sunday, their meeting was only confirmed on Thursday night, when Trump posted a screenshot of a text message from President Zelensky saying it was "important for us to have a personal contact and to understand each other 100%".

There have been tensions all week between Zelensky and the Republican party ahead of November's US presidential election.
Some Republicans were angered by Zelensky's visit to an arms factory in Biden's hometown of Scranton, Pennsylvania, with top Democrats, including state Governor Josh Shapiro, earlier this week.
Zelensky's trip to the key swing state was labelled by leading Republicans as a partisan campaign event. In a public letter, House Speaker Mike Johnson said the visit was "designed to help Democrats" and claimed it amounted to "election interference".

In contrast, Zelensky recently told the New Yorker magazine that he believes Trump "doesn't really know how to stop the war" and called Trump's running mate JD Vance "too radical" and "dangerous" for suggesting that Ukraine should give up territory to end the war, saying it would spark conflict around the world.
When asked about Zelensky's comments on Thursday, Trump replied: "I do believe I disagree with him. He doesn't know me."

The United States has asked Ukraine whether it would withdraw troops from parts of the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, signaling a potential shift in President Donald Trump's previous opposition to Kyiv joining the Western military alliance.
Zelensky told reporters Friday that American negotiators raised the question for the first time, though he added that the discussions have not yielded a concrete proposal.
"The Americans asked: 'If Ukraine joins NATO, will Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" Zelensky said in remarks released Saturday.
The Ukrainian president stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian, while also rejecting the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution.
"If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway."
Russian President Vladimir Putin has long said NATO membership for Ukraine is a red line for his country, citing the issue as one reason for launching his invasion of Kyiv in February 2022.
Earlier this week, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials met in Abu Dhabi for their first trilateral negotiations in nine months. Meanwhile, European officials held separate talks with U.S. and Ukrainian counterparts there without engaging directly with Moscow.
The inquiry involves land in the Donbas that Ukrainian forces still control and Russian troops have failed to capture. Agreeing to pull back would force Ukrainians to weigh ceding territory their military has fought to defend against the promise of alliance protection from future Russian aggression.
_Newsweek_ has reached out to the State Department for comment.
texts.1:
## Shifting Messaging on NATO
The reported question marks a notable departure from Trump's earlier stance. In an August 2025 interview with Fox News, Trump ruled out Kyiv's entry into the alliance, saying, "They're not going to be a part of NATO." At the time, he suggested European nations should take the lead in defending Ukraine and ruled out deploying U.S. troops to protect its borders.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also downplayed the prospect of membership last month, citing the requirement for unanimous agreement among all NATO allies.
"Right now, we're simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict, if that's possible," Rubio said.
A joint statement on November 10 following talks among U.S., Ukrainian and European officials endorsed credible security guarantees for Kyiv and affirmed that "a strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defence," though it stopped short of backing Ukrainian membership. NATO maintains that Ukraine's future lies within the alliance, provided members agree and Kyiv meets necessary conditions.
U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff (right), Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speak to the media at the airport in Dublin on November 12. (AP Photo/Peter Morrison).
texts.2:
## Package of Guarantees
Zelensky said Kyiv is discussing a broader framework that includes security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, weapons and funding for Ukraine's military, and postwar reconstruction funds. Any formal proposal would have to be presented to the Ukrainian public, he said.
"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?" he said. "I have no right to make that decision on my own. But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet."
He reiterated that Kyiv will not recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied territory, meaning a troop withdrawal would leave Ukraine's claims to the land unresolved.
Zelensky also warned that Putin could use the negotiations to weaken NATO and redraw European borders, turning talks on ending the nearly five-year war into a wider bargain over continental security.
"Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."
Zelensky later added: "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."
texts.3:
## Europe Seeks a Seat at the Table
Addressing European leaders in Dublin on Thursday, Zelensky urged the bloc to secure a permanent role in the negotiations, characterizing U.S.-Russian discussions as "more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia."
Washington has acknowledged the talks carry wider implications. Jared Kushner, Trump's envoy and son-in-law, said European participation would allow negotiators to address "broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia."
Zelensky's remarks followed an agreement by EU leaders on Friday that Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland — known as the E5 — will represent Europe alongside EU institutions at the next round of peace talks, European Council President António Costa announced.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged allies on Friday to sustain pressure on the Kremlin.
"The best way to get Russia to the table is to keep up our support for Ukraine and to keep maximum pressure on Russia," she said.
The European Commission is preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia and a financing proposal for Ukraine ahead of a November 26–27 European Council summit.

Title: Zelensky says U.S. raised territory-for-NATO trade-off
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The United States has asked Ukraine whether it would withdraw troops from parts of the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, signaling a potential shift in President Donald Trump's previous opposition to Kyiv joining the Western military alliance.
Zelensky told reporters Friday that American negotiators raised the question for the first time, though he added that the discussions have not yielded a concrete proposal.
"The Americans asked: 'If Ukraine joins NATO, will Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?'" Zelensky said in remarks released Saturday.
The Ukrainian president stressed that any arrangement would not involve recognizing occupied territories as Russian, while also rejecting the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality, saying that would require changing the country's constitution.
"If Putin expects Ukraine's neutrality to be enshrined, that's not going to happen," he said. "We're not in NATO right now anyway."
Russian President Vladimir Putin has long said NATO membership for Ukraine is a red line for his country, citing the issue as one reason for launching his invasion of Kyiv in February 2022.
Earlier this week, Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials met in Abu Dhabi for their first trilateral negotiations in nine months. Meanwhile, European officials held separate talks with U.S. and Ukrainian counterparts there without engaging directly with Moscow.
The inquiry involves land in the Donbas that Ukrainian forces still control and Russian troops have failed to capture. Agreeing to pull back would force Ukrainians to weigh ceding territory their military has fought to defend against the promise of alliance protection from future Russian aggression.
_Newsweek_ has reached out to the State Department for comment.

## Shifting Messaging on NATO
The reported question marks a notable departure from Trump's earlier stance. In an August 2025 interview with Fox News, Trump ruled out Kyiv's entry into the alliance, saying, "They're not going to be a part of NATO." At the time, he suggested European nations should take the lead in defending Ukraine and ruled out deploying U.S. troops to protect its borders.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio also downplayed the prospect of membership last month, citing the requirement for unanimous agreement among all NATO allies.
"Right now, we're simply focused, when it comes to Ukraine, on the ending of this conflict, if that's possible," Rubio said.
A joint statement on November 10 following talks among U.S., Ukrainian and European officials endorsed credible security guarantees for Kyiv and affirmed that "a strong NATO will remain central to Euro-Atlantic collective defence," though it stopped short of backing Ukrainian membership. NATO maintains that Ukraine's future lies within the alliance, provided members agree and Kyiv meets necessary conditions.
U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff (right), Jared Kushner, President Donald Trump's son-in-law, and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky speak to the media at the airport in Dublin on November 12. (AP Photo/Peter Morrison).

## Package of Guarantees
Zelensky said Kyiv is discussing a broader framework that includes security guarantees from NATO and the European Union, weapons and funding for Ukraine's military, and postwar reconstruction funds. Any formal proposal would have to be presented to the Ukrainian public, he said.
"If the American side confirms precisely this to us, together with other NATO partners, then I will ask our Ukrainian society what it thinks: do we accept it or not?" he said. "I have no right to make that decision on my own. But we need specifics, and we don't have them yet."
He reiterated that Kyiv will not recognize Russian sovereignty over occupied territory, meaning a troop withdrawal would leave Ukraine's claims to the land unresolved.
Zelensky also warned that Putin could use the negotiations to weaken NATO and redraw European borders, turning talks on ending the nearly five-year war into a wider bargain over continental security.
"Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe," he said. "This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations."
Zelensky later added: "Real security in Europe means the EU and NATO. That's it. There is no other security in Europe."

## Europe Seeks a Seat at the Table
Addressing European leaders in Dublin on Thursday, Zelensky urged the bloc to secure a permanent role in the negotiations, characterizing U.S.-Russian discussions as "more about some kind of new security framework between Europe and Russia."
Washington has acknowledged the talks carry wider implications. Jared Kushner, Trump's envoy and son-in-law, said European participation would allow negotiators to address "broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia."
Zelensky's remarks followed an agreement by EU leaders on Friday that Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland — known as the E5 — will represent Europe alongside EU institutions at the next round of peace talks, European Council President António Costa announced.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged allies on Friday to sustain pressure on the Kremlin.
"The best way to get Russia to the table is to keep up our support for Ukraine and to keep maximum pressure on Russia," she said.
The European Commission is preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia and a financing proposal for Ukraine ahead of a November 26–27 European Council summit.

April 3, 1962  
Ukraine’s “Secession” From USSR  
Simulated By SUSTA Delegates  
At Model U.N. General Assembly

## [PDF page 211]
NEW YORK, N.Y. (Special) – The delegation of SUSTA (Federation of  
Ukrainian Student Organizations of America) drew the attention of more  
than 800 delegates and faculty advisors to the plight of the Ukrainian people  
and their enslavement in the USSR by staging a well-prepared “mock seces-  
sion” of Ukraine from the Soviet Union during the plenary session of the  
35th Annual Mid-Atlantic Model General Assembly. More than 90 colleges  
and universities sent their student delegations and faculty advisors to these  
“mock sessions,” which took place on March 23-25, 1962, at the Commodore  
Hotel in New York City. Each school represented a country-member of the  
United Nations.  
The SUSTA delegation was headed by Bohdan Futej of Cleveland, Ohio,  
and represented Ukraine. SUSTA was the only non-college participant in the  
Model General Assembly, which fact created some initial technical difficul-  
ties, but eventually the Ukrainian delegation won full-fledged membership  
for the duration of the entire session.  
Availing himself of the privilege of explaining the vote of the Ukrainian  
delegation on a resolution before the Assembly session on Sunday, Mr. Futej  
read a purported telegram from the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the new  
government of the Ukrainian National Republic in Kiev announcing the  
“secession” of Ukraine from the USSR. A similar telegram was sent to the  
president of the Model General Assembly, Edward Keynes of Queen’s  
College.  
Mr. Futej was ruled out of order, and the Canadian delegation, repre-  
sented by St. Peter’s College of Jersey City, N.J., introduced a motion of cen-  
sure against the Ukrainian delegation for bringing up an item which was not  
on the agenda of the Assembly. Although the motion was carried, the inter-  
vention of the Ukrainian delegation provided an opportunity to introduce the  
Ukrainian issue into the general discussion which lasted for over 35 minutes  
and brought an entire new aspect of Soviet Russian colonialism to the partic-  
ipants of the Assembly.  
Meanwhile, over 950 copies of a special “overseas edition” of the Voice of  
Free Ukraine were distributed to the participants, the New York press and  

## [PDF page 211]
foreign embassies by the members of the Ukrainian student groups from  
New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Syracuse. The issue contained an  
“Act of Secession” and the address of the “President” of the Ukrainian
211

## [PDF page 212]
National Republic, in which the crimes and abuses committed by the  
Kremlin over the Ukrainian people were enumerated and well documented.  
The immediate reaction of student delegates and faculty advisors was that  
the issue of Soviet Russian colonialism within the USSR and its satellites  
should be discussed at the next Model General Assembly session, inasmuch  
as the Canadian Prime Minister John G. Diefenbaker, in his speech on  
November 22, 1961 (The Globe and Mail, November 23, 1961) in Toronto,  
indicated that Canada will introduce the issue at the next session of the U.N.  
General Assembly this fall.
February 16, 1963  
Metropolitan Joseph Slipy,  
Martyred Head Of Ukrainian Catholic Church,  
Released From Soviet Dungeons,  
Receives Warm Welcome  
From Pope John XXIII In Rome
SPENT 18 YEARS IN JAIL AND CONCENTRATION CAMPS  
IN DEFENSE OF THE CHURCH AND THE UKRAINIAN PEOPLE

## [PDF page 212]
VATICAN CITY, February 10 (Combined Wire Services) – Metropolitan  
Joseph Slipy, Archbishop of Lviv, western Ukraine, arrived here last night after  
his release from 18 years’ imprisonment and detention in the Soviet Union.  
Metropolitan Slipy, accompanied by Amleto Giovanni Cardinal Cicognani,  
Vatican Secretary of State, and Gustav Cardinal Tests, was received this  
afternoon by Pope John XXIII for almost an hour.  
“A touching consolation arrived last night from Eastern Europe,” the  
Pope said in an emotional-charged voice. “We thank God for this as a thing  
which in Divine secrecy could prepare the Holy Church and forthright souls  
for an outburst of sincere faith and of a simple and peaceful apostolate.”  
Metropolitan Slipy who will be 71 years of age on Sunday, February 17,  
1963, was arrested just a few months after he was appointed Archbishop of  
the Ukrainians in Lviv in November 1944, following the death of  
Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky.  
He and other Ukrainian Bishops were tried in April 1946 on charges of  
“collaboration” during the German occupation of Ukraine. In 1947 the  
Moscow radio announced he had been sentenced to prison. Subsequently he  
was tried again on charges of sending secret pastoral letters to his faithful and  
was sent to Siberian slave labor camps. For years there was no news from him  
at all. In 1958 it was reported that he was working as a servant in an old peo-
212

## [PDF page 213]
ples’ home in central Siberia. In 1960 word got out that he had been offered an  
important post with the Soviet Orthodox Church, that of Patriarch, if he  
would renounce his faith. Instead of accepting the offer, he denounced the  
“corruption” of the Soviet-dominated Russian Orthodox Church.  
When Pope John XXIII named three cardinals in pectore (in the secrecy of  
his own heart), it was rumored that all three were impeded behind the Iron  
Curtain and that Archbishop Slipy was one of the three. The in pectore cardi-  
nals are, of course, not listed with the other cardinals and only the Pope knows  
their identity.  
Archbishop Slipy’s long suffering, martyrdom and heroic anti-  
Communist stand won him the reputation of a stalwart Christian martyr.  
Many thought that he was dead, along with the other nine Ukrainian  
Catholic Bishops who were captured and put to torture by the Soviet NKVD  
and MVD after World War II.  
There was considerable speculation about the Soviet move in releasing  
Archbishop Slipy. Pope John XXIII explained only that “the Soviet govern-  
ment had released the prelate and allowed him to make his way to Rome,  
where he will live in a religious community.” The event was seen in some  
quarters as another action by the USSR in an attempt to improve relations  
between the Vatican and Moscow. It followed an exchange of messages  
between Pope John XXIII and Khrushchev on the Pope’s most recent birth-  
day and on other occasions.
Metropolitan Joseph Slipy (left) during his years in Ukraine and  
(right) in Rome in January 1965 awaiting the delivery of the papal  
bull announcing his elevation to cardinal.
213

## [PDF page 214]
Other sources pointed to two other developments to help explain the sur-  
prise release. The arrival of two Russian Orthodox Churchmen as observers  
to the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council last October followed the visit to  
Moscow of Msgr. John Willebrands, S.J., of the Secretariat to Promote  
Christian Unity. These initial contacts, it is believed, may have led to new  
results, including the release of Archbishop Slipy.  
Another development was the stand taken by 15 Ukrainian Catholic bishops  
of the free world attending the Ecumenical Council, who denounced the pres-  
ence of the two Russian Orthodox churchmen while Archbishop Slipy was still in  
a Soviet jail. Their protest may have started a chain reaction which led to the  
release of the Ukrainian Archbishop. Il Tempo of Rome, in discussing a possible  
reason for Archbishop Slipy’s release, said that Slipy early last year was offered  
the post of orthodox Patriarch of Moscow, but the Archbishop refused and sent a  
stern protest to the Soviet government over this “attempt at corruption.”  
It is recalled that on November 22, 1962, fifteen Ukrainian Archbishops and  
Bishops attending the Ecumenical Council in Rome issued a strong statement  
protesting the presence of two Russian Orthodox observers, contrasting their  
presence with the continued detention and persecution of Metropolitan Joseph  
Slipy. “The presence of the two Soviet observers at the Council has disconcerted  
true believers, astounded many Council fathers and engendered a feeling of dis-  
content and indignation among the faithful everywhere,” the statement said.
September 13, 1963  
3,000 Faithful, With 50 Priests,  
Led By Metropolitan Senyshyn  
Take Part In Blessing And Dedication  
Of New Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral

## [PDF page 214]
PHILADELPHIA, Pa. (Special) – On Sunday, September 8, 1963, the bless-  
ing and dedication of the new Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral took place here with  
an impressive ceremony, attended by some 3,000 faithful and 50 Ukrainian  
Catholic priests from the archdiocese. The act of blessing was performed by the  
Most Rev. Ambrose Senyshyn, OSBM, Archbishop of Philadelphia and  
Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Catholic Church in the United States.  
After the moleben an impressive procession marched to the site of the  
new cathedral headed by the units of Ukrainian youth organizations such as  
Plast and SUMA in their uniforms, and by representatives of Ukrainian cen-  
tral organizations, members of the Providence Association, the “Soyuz  
Ukrainok” and the local post of the Catholic War Veterans, as well as school  
children led by the nuns. The moleben was officiated by Metropolitan
214

## [PDF page 215]
Senyshyn, who was assisted by Rev. M. Charyna and Rev. William Losten.  
Metropolitan Senyshyn delivered an inspiring and penetrating sermon, in  
which he underscored the historical significance of Philadelphia, a “City of  
Brotherly Love” and the cradle of American independence, where such promi-  
nent Americans as Betsy Ross, Benjamin Franklin, George Washington and  
Thomas Jefferson lived and planned the foundation of the American republic.  
Philadelphia also has a special significance for Ukrainians, Metropolitan  
Senyshyn continued. It was here that the first foundations of the Ukrainian  
Catholic Church in the United States were laid down by Bishop Soter  
Ortynsky and his successor, Metropolitan Constantine Bohachevsky. In con-  
clusion, the Metropolitan bestowed his blessings upon those in attendance.  
Among the representatives of Ukrainian organizations taking part in the  
ceremony were Monsignor Stephen Cehansky, president of the Providence  
Association of Ukrainian Catholics; Stepan Sprynsky and Teofil Kulchytsky,  
recording secretary and financial secretary of the Providence Association,  
respectively; Joseph Lesawyer, supreme president of the UNA; Prof. Roman  
Smal-Stocki, president of the Shevchenko Scientific Society, Mrs. Helen  
Lototsky, president of “Soyuz Ukrainok”; as well as Eugene Zyblikevych and  
Mstyslav Dolnytsky, editors of America, and Anthony Dragan, editor of Svoboda.  
Plans for the new Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral, which will cost about  
$3,000,000, were drawn by Julian Jastremsky, prominent Ukrainian American  
architect, who was also present at the blessing and dedication ceremonies.
October 19, 1963  
Metropolitan Slipy Proposes Creation  
Of Ukrainian Patriarchate

## [PDF page 215]
VATICAN CITY – Metropolitan Joseph Slipy, Archbishop of Lviv and  
Primate of Ukraine released last January after 18 years in Soviet jails and  
concentration camps, addressed the Ecumenical Council on Friday, October  
11, for the first time since his arrival in the Holy City. The Council Fathers  
applauded thunderously when the Archbishop rose to speak despite a  
reminder from Giacomo Cardinal Lercardo of Bologna, who was presiding at  
the session in St. Peter’s Basilica, that applause was out of order.  
In an emotional address the 72-year-old Archbishop told the Council  
Fathers that he thanked God for “the almost miraculous possibility of taking  
part in this council,” and then startled them by asking that his archbishopric  
be raised to the status of a patriarchate, saying that such a step would do  
much to please and interest the Orthodox, who take great pride in the patri-  
archal structure of their own Churches. It must be assumed that the  
Archbishop’s statement reflects the general attitude of all Ukrainian

A cross standing where Wydymer village once existed. The sign reads: “Here was the village of Wydymer. In 1943 – destroyed. The Poles have scattered across the whole world. 1943-2006”.

Gordian Knot. The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lw w) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian flags appeared on government offices and announcements circulated the city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic ( established with Lviv as its capital. For those Leopolitans who dreamed of a free Poland, the prospect of becoming West Ukrainian citizens was unac ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and increased desires to actively oppose these developments. That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting, giving rise to the legend of the Lw w Eaglets. On November 22, 191 due to resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left Lviv. This was, however, only the beginning of the Polish-Ukrainian war, or rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war. By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units went on the offensive. Partial forces from General J zef Haller’s army, which had arrived from France, were used for this purpose (though promises had been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in Galicia). Polish pressure forced the bleeding units to retreat behind the Zbruch River, which was to form the southeastern border of a reborn Poland. The last units crossed over on July 16, 1919. The government led by Yevhen Petrushevych went first to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and then into exile. The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lw w) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian flags appeared on government offices and announcements circulated the city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic ( established with Lviv as its capital. For those Leopolitans who dreamed of a free Poland, the prospect of becoming West Ukrainian citizens was unac ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and increased desires to actively oppose these developments. That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting, giving rise to the legend of the Lw w Eaglets. On November 22, 191 due to resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left Lviv. This was, however, only the beginning of the Polish-Ukrainian war, or rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war. By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units went on the offensive. Partial forces from General J zef Haller’s army, which had arrived from France, were used for this purpose (though promises had been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in Galicia). Polish pressure forced the bleeding units to retreat behind the Zbruch River, which was to form the southeastern border of a reborn Poland. The last units crossed over on July 16, 1919. The incorporation of the into the Polish Republic was accepted by the leader of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Symon Petliura, who wanted thereby to save Ukrainian statehood on the Dnieper River.

April 3, 1962  
Ukraine’s “Secession” From USSR  
Simulated By SUSTA Delegates  
At Model U.N. General Assembly
texts.417:
## [PDF page 211]
NEW YORK, N.Y. (Special) – The delegation of SUSTA (Federation of  
Ukrainian Student Organizations of America) drew the attention of more  
than 800 delegates and faculty advisors to the plight of the Ukrainian people  
and their enslavement in the USSR by staging a well-prepared “mock seces-  
sion” of Ukraine from the Soviet Union during the plenary session of the  
35th Annual Mid-Atlantic Model General Assembly. More than 90 colleges  
and universities sent their student delegations and faculty advisors to these  
“mock sessions,” which took place on March 23-25, 1962, at the Commodore  
Hotel in New York City. Each school represented a country-member of the  
United Nations.  
The SUSTA delegation was headed by Bohdan Futej of Cleveland, Ohio,  
and represented Ukraine. SUSTA was the only non-college participant in the  
Model General Assembly, which fact created some initial technical difficul-  
ties, but eventually the Ukrainian delegation won full-fledged membership  
for the duration of the entire session.  
Availing himself of the privilege of explaining the vote of the Ukrainian  
delegation on a resolution before the Assembly session on Sunday, Mr. Futej  
read a purported telegram from the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the new  
government of the Ukrainian National Republic in Kiev announcing the  
“secession” of Ukraine from the USSR. A similar telegram was sent to the  
president of the Model General Assembly, Edward Keynes of Queen’s  
College.  
Mr. Futej was ruled out of order, and the Canadian delegation, repre-  
sented by St. Peter’s College of Jersey City, N.J., introduced a motion of cen-  
sure against the Ukrainian delegation for bringing up an item which was not  
on the agenda of the Assembly. Although the motion was carried, the inter-  
vention of the Ukrainian delegation provided an opportunity to introduce the  
Ukrainian issue into the general discussion which lasted for over 35 minutes  
and brought an entire new aspect of Soviet Russian colonialism to the partic-  
ipants of the Assembly.  
Meanwhile, over 950 copies of a special “overseas edition” of the Voice of  
Free Ukraine were distributed to the participants, the New York press and
texts.418:
## [PDF page 211]
foreign embassies by the members of the Ukrainian student groups from  
New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore and Syracuse. The issue contained an  
“Act of Secession” and the address of the “President” of the Ukrainian
211

## [PDF page 212]
National Republic, in which the crimes and abuses committed by the  
Kremlin over the Ukrainian people were enumerated and well documented.  
The immediate reaction of student delegates and faculty advisors was that  
the issue of Soviet Russian colonialism within the USSR and its satellites  
should be discussed at the next Model General Assembly session, inasmuch  
as the Canadian Prime Minister John G. Diefenbaker, in his speech on  
November 22, 1961 (The Globe and Mail, November 23, 1961) in Toronto,  
indicated that Canada will introduce the issue at the next session of the U.N.  
General Assembly this fall.
February 16, 1963  
Metropolitan Joseph Slipy,  
Martyred Head Of Ukrainian Catholic Church,  
Released From Soviet Dungeons,  
Receives Warm Welcome  
From Pope John XXIII In Rome
SPENT 18 YEARS IN JAIL AND CONCENTRATION CAMPS  
IN DEFENSE OF THE CHURCH AND THE UKRAINIAN PEOPLE
texts.420:
## [PDF page 212]
VATICAN CITY, February 10 (Combined Wire Services) – Metropolitan  
Joseph Slipy, Archbishop of Lviv, western Ukraine, arrived here last night after  
his release from 18 years’ imprisonment and detention in the Soviet Union.  
Metropolitan Slipy, accompanied by Amleto Giovanni Cardinal Cicognani,  
Vatican Secretary of State, and Gustav Cardinal Tests, was received this  
afternoon by Pope John XXIII for almost an hour.  
“A touching consolation arrived last night from Eastern Europe,” the  
Pope said in an emotional-charged voice. “We thank God for this as a thing  
which in Divine secrecy could prepare the Holy Church and forthright souls  
for an outburst of sincere faith and of a simple and peaceful apostolate.”  
Metropolitan Slipy who will be 71 years of age on Sunday, February 17,  
1963, was arrested just a few months after he was appointed Archbishop of  
the Ukrainians in Lviv in November 1944, following the death of  
Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky.  
He and other Ukrainian Bishops were tried in April 1946 on charges of  
“collaboration” during the German occupation of Ukraine. In 1947 the  
Moscow radio announced he had been sentenced to prison. Subsequently he  
was tried again on charges of sending secret pastoral letters to his faithful and  
was sent to Siberian slave labor camps. For years there was no news from him  
at all. In 1958 it was reported that he was working as a servant in an old peo-
212
texts.421:
## [PDF page 213]
ples’ home in central Siberia. In 1960 word got out that he had been offered an  
important post with the Soviet Orthodox Church, that of Patriarch, if he  
would renounce his faith. Instead of accepting the offer, he denounced the  
“corruption” of the Soviet-dominated Russian Orthodox Church.  
When Pope John XXIII named three cardinals in pectore (in the secrecy of  
his own heart), it was rumored that all three were impeded behind the Iron  
Curtain and that Archbishop Slipy was one of the three. The in pectore cardi-  
nals are, of course, not listed with the other cardinals and only the Pope knows  
their identity.  
Archbishop Slipy’s long suffering, martyrdom and heroic anti-  
Communist stand won him the reputation of a stalwart Christian martyr.  
Many thought that he was dead, along with the other nine Ukrainian  
Catholic Bishops who were captured and put to torture by the Soviet NKVD  
and MVD after World War II.  
There was considerable speculation about the Soviet move in releasing  
Archbishop Slipy. Pope John XXIII explained only that “the Soviet govern-  
ment had released the prelate and allowed him to make his way to Rome,  
where he will live in a religious community.” The event was seen in some  
quarters as another action by the USSR in an attempt to improve relations  
between the Vatican and Moscow. It followed an exchange of messages  
between Pope John XXIII and Khrushchev on the Pope’s most recent birth-  
day and on other occasions.
Metropolitan Joseph Slipy (left) during his years in Ukraine and  
(right) in Rome in January 1965 awaiting the delivery of the papal  
bull announcing his elevation to cardinal.
213
texts.422:
## [PDF page 214]
Other sources pointed to two other developments to help explain the sur-  
prise release. The arrival of two Russian Orthodox Churchmen as observers  
to the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council last October followed the visit to  
Moscow of Msgr. John Willebrands, S.J., of the Secretariat to Promote  
Christian Unity. These initial contacts, it is believed, may have led to new  
results, including the release of Archbishop Slipy.  
Another development was the stand taken by 15 Ukrainian Catholic bishops  
of the free world attending the Ecumenical Council, who denounced the pres-  
ence of the two Russian Orthodox churchmen while Archbishop Slipy was still in  
a Soviet jail. Their protest may have started a chain reaction which led to the  
release of the Ukrainian Archbishop. Il Tempo of Rome, in discussing a possible  
reason for Archbishop Slipy’s release, said that Slipy early last year was offered  
the post of orthodox Patriarch of Moscow, but the Archbishop refused and sent a  
stern protest to the Soviet government over this “attempt at corruption.”  
It is recalled that on November 22, 1962, fifteen Ukrainian Archbishops and  
Bishops attending the Ecumenical Council in Rome issued a strong statement  
protesting the presence of two Russian Orthodox observers, contrasting their  
presence with the continued detention and persecution of Metropolitan Joseph  
Slipy. “The presence of the two Soviet observers at the Council has disconcerted  
true believers, astounded many Council fathers and engendered a feeling of dis-  
content and indignation among the faithful everywhere,” the statement said.
September 13, 1963  
3,000 Faithful, With 50 Priests,  
Led By Metropolitan Senyshyn  
Take Part In Blessing And Dedication  
Of New Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral
texts.423:
## [PDF page 214]
PHILADELPHIA, Pa. (Special) – On Sunday, September 8, 1963, the bless-  
ing and dedication of the new Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral took place here with  
an impressive ceremony, attended by some 3,000 faithful and 50 Ukrainian  
Catholic priests from the archdiocese. The act of blessing was performed by the  
Most Rev. Ambrose Senyshyn, OSBM, Archbishop of Philadelphia and  
Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Catholic Church in the United States.  
After the moleben an impressive procession marched to the site of the

Gordian Knot. The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic On the first of November 1918, the feeling that must have dominated among the Poles living in Lviv (Polish: Lw w) was astonishment. On that day, Ukrainian flags appeared on government offices and announcements circulated the city, indicating that the West Ukrainian People’s Republic ( established with Lviv as its capital. For those Leopolitans who dreamed of a free Poland, the prospect of becoming West Ukrainian citizens was unac ceptable. The fact that they had been overtaken in the process of creating a state by the Ukrainians, a national group that many believed did not exist but was “invented by the Austrians to spite the Poles”, aroused astonishment and increased desires to actively oppose these developments. That same day, Polish underground groups spontaneously began launching counteroperations. The initially uncoordinated skirmishes quickly turned into fierce street battles. Among the ranks of Polish units were many youths under seventeen years of age who bravely and sacrificially took part in the fighting, giving rise to the legend of the Lw w Eaglets. On November 22, 191 due to resistance and arrival of reinforcements to the city – the Ukrainian army left Lviv. This was, however, only the beginning of the Polish-Ukrainian war, or rather the Polish-West Ukrainian war. By March 1919, the Ukrainian Galician Army had attempted three maneu vers to regain Lviv, failing each time. In the following weeks, Polish Army units went on the offensive. Partial forces from General J zef Haller’s army, which had arrived from France, were used for this purpose (though promises had been made to the Western powers that these units would not be deployed in Galicia). Polish pressure forced the bleeding units to retreat behind the Zbruch River, which was to form the southeastern border of a reborn Poland. The last units crossed over on July 16, 1919. The government led by Yevhen Petrushevych went first to Kamianets-Podilskyi, and then into exile. The incorporation of the into the Polish Republic was accepted by the leader of the Ukrainian People’s Republic, Symon Petliura, who wanted thereby to save Ukrainian statehood on the Dnieper River.

As is known, his hopes were dashed by the unfolding of the Polish-Soviet War and the Peace of Riga signed in March 1921.

Despite military defeat, western Ukrainians did not lose hope for indepen dence. The Poles had trouble getting the victorious powers, mainly France and England, to agree to Poland’s incorporation of Eastern Galicia. In June 1919 Poland was granted only the right of temporary administration over the region, while serious consideration was given to the idea that its fate should be decided by inhabitants themselves in a plebiscite held under the auspices of the League of Nations. Though Lviv was a Polish city, Ukrainians were the majority in the remainder of Eastern Galicia. According to the 1931 census, Lviv was inhabited by 157,000 Poles, 99,000 Jews, and just under 50,000 Ukrainians, yet of the 4,729,515 people living in all of Eastern Galicia, 2,847,844 were Greek Catholics (almost entirely Ukrainians), 1,350,978 declared themselves to be Roman Catholics (Poles), and 490,459 professed Judaism (Jews). The results of any plebiscite would have therefore certainly been unfavourable for Poland. The authorities of the Second Polish Republic, realizing this danger, began to strengthen Polish identity in the Kresy (Polish for “borderlands”) imme diately following the victory. Government offices were first to be Polonized, with all individuals refusing to swear an oath of allegiance to the Polish state being removed. Next, the Ukrainian chairs at the University of Lviv were abol ished and a principle by which only those Polish citizens who had served in the Polish Army could study there was adopted. Finally, on December 5, 1920, all of Galicia was divided into four voivodeships (provinces): Krak w, Lw w,
The Ukrainian Problem in the Second Polish Republic

w. A photograph taken in November 1918.
Tarnopol, and Stanisł w. The borders of these provinces were shifted west ward to change their demographic composition in favour of the Polish popula tion. Thus, Lw w Voivodeship came to include powiats (counties) inhabited mainly by Poles: Rzesz w, Kolbuszowa, Krosno, and Tarnobrzeg. Eastern Galicia was officially named Eastern Lesser Poland (Wschodnia Małopolska Moreover, in December 1920 the Legislative Sejm (Poland’s parliament) passed a law that granted farmsteads in Volhynia on favourable financial terms to deserving soldiers and war invalids from central Poland, who were often set tled in isolated settlements. These actions provoked opposition from a large portion of the Ukrainian population. The Ukrainian political parties did not recognize Polish statehood, accepting only the exiled government as a legal authority. A similar position was taken, among others, by the leader of the Greek Catholic Church, Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytskyi. A call for passive resistance went out, namely in the form of boycotts of the census being organized by the Polish authori ties, conscription into the army, and elections to the Sejm (November 1922). In October 1919 circles of underground Ukrainian education began forming, and July 1921 an underground university (existing until 1925) opened its doors.

The transfer of farms to Polish colonists was particularly resented – local peas ants commonly believed that the colonists appropriated land that should belong to them instead. The Ukrainians by no means intended to limit themselves to passive resis tance. Some Ukrainian officers and soldiers refused to lay down arms. In the summer of 1920, the underground Ukrainian Military Organization (UVO) was formed, headed by Colonel Yevhen Konovalets. The name of the organization rather inadvertently alluded to the Polish Military Organization ( bers of the UVO would later use Polish experiences in the struggle for inde pendence as a touchstone. Initially, UVO subordinated itself to Petrushevych’s government-in-exile in Vienna. Immediately after its creation, the organization began operations aimed at opposing the incorporation of Eastern Galicia and other disputed territories into the Republic of Poland. The first UVO terrorist act was carried out on November 25, 1921, in Lviv: an unsuccessful attempt on Marshal J zef Piłsudski’s life (with the accompanying Lviv Voivode Kazimierz Grabowski being wounded). Sabotage actions carried out under Konovalets’ direct leadership in the summer and autumn of 1922 were more serious. Grain stacks and farms of newly settled colonists and other Poles were set on fire. Bombs were planted at police and railroad stations, military warehouses, and on telegraph and telephone poles. Operations included the burning of mili tary warehouses near Przemyśl and police buildings in Yavoriv, Grdek, Uhniv and Lubacz w. As part of a liquidation of “traitors”, on October 15, 1922, in Kamianka Strumilova ( day UVO members killed Sydir Tverdohlib, a Ukrainian poet and journalist, leader of the Agrarian Ukrainian Peasants’ Party and candidate for the Polish Sejm. This sabotage campaign, supported by communist circles, lasted several months. Three hundred acts of sabotage and diversion were likely committed. Police statistics list 223 acts of sabotage in 1922, including 17 attacks on officials (with five killed), 15 attacks on Ukrainian conciliators (nine deaths), 129 acts of arson and robberies, 27 sabotages of state facilities, and 35 telephone and telegraph wire cutting incidents.

All this, however, failed to alter the Ukrainians’ position on the international stage. On March 14, 1923, the Council of Ambassadors, which had succeeded the Supreme War Council at the Paris Peace Conference, granted Eastern Galicia to Poland with the expectation that the local government of these ter ritories would be given certain autonomous rights. The decision of the Council of Ambassadors seemed to close the issue of Poland’s eastern border, at least in the perception of most western Ukrainians. This quickly eroded the authority of the Petrushevych government, with which even the UVO ceased coopera tion in its determination to continue its desperate struggle.

Ukrainian Student Organizations of America) drew the attention of more

and represented Ukraine. SUSTA was the only non-college participant in the

for the duration of the entire session.  
Availing himself of the privilege of explaining the vote of the Ukrainian

read a purported telegram from the Minister of Foreign Affairs of the new  
government of the Ukrainian National Republic in Kiev announcing the  
“secession” of Ukraine from the USSR. A similar telegram was sent to the  
president of the Model General Assembly, Edward Keynes of Queen’s  
College.  
Mr. Futej was ruled out of order, and the Canadian delegation, repre-  
sented by St. Peter’s College of Jersey City, N.J., introduced a motion of cen-  
sure against the Ukrainian delegation for bringing up an item which was not  
on the agenda of the Assembly. Although the motion was carried, the inter-  
vention of the Ukrainian delegation provided an opportunity to introduce the  
Ukrainian issue into the general discussion which lasted for over 35 minutes  
and brought an entire new aspect of Soviet Russian colonialism to the partic-  
ipants of the Assembly.

VATICAN CITY, February 10 (Combined Wire Services) – Metropolitan  
Joseph Slipy, Archbishop of Lviv, western Ukraine, arrived here last night after  
his release from 18 years’ imprisonment and detention in the Soviet Union.  
Metropolitan Slipy, accompanied by Amleto Giovanni Cardinal Cicognani,  
Vatican Secretary of State, and Gustav Cardinal Tests, was received this  
afternoon by Pope John XXIII for almost an hour.  
“A touching consolation arrived last night from Eastern Europe,” the  
Pope said in an emotional-charged voice. “We thank God for this as a thing  
which in Divine secrecy could prepare the Holy Church and forthright souls  
for an outburst of sincere faith and of a simple and peaceful apostolate.”  
Metropolitan Slipy who will be 71 years of age on Sunday, February 17,  
1963, was arrested just a few months after he was appointed Archbishop of  
the Ukrainians in Lviv in November 1944, following the death of  
Metropolitan Andrey Sheptytsky.  
He and other Ukrainian Bishops were tried in April 1946 on charges of  
“collaboration” during the German occupation of Ukraine. In 1947 the  
Moscow radio announced he had been sentenced to prison. Subsequently he  
was tried again on charges of sending secret pastoral letters to his faithful and  
was sent to Siberian slave labor camps. For years there was no news from him  
at all. In 1958 it was reported that he was working as a servant in an old peo-
212

## [PDF page 213]
ples’ home in central Siberia. In 1960 word got out that he had been offered an  
important post with the Soviet Orthodox Church, that of Patriarch, if he  
would renounce his faith. Instead of accepting the offer, he denounced the  
“corruption” of the Soviet-dominated Russian Orthodox Church.  
When Pope John XXIII named three cardinals in pectore (in the secrecy of  
his own heart), it was rumored that all three were impeded behind the Iron  
Curtain and that Archbishop Slipy was one of the three. The in pectore cardi-  
nals are, of course, not listed with the other cardinals and only the Pope knows  
their identity.  
Archbishop Slipy’s long suffering, martyrdom and heroic anti-  
Communist stand won him the reputation of a stalwart Christian martyr.  
Many thought that he was dead, along with the other nine Ukrainian  
Catholic Bishops who were captured and put to torture by the Soviet NKVD  
and MVD after World War II.  
There was considerable speculation about the Soviet move in releasing  
Archbishop Slipy. Pope John XXIII explained only that “the Soviet govern-  
ment had released the prelate and allowed him to make his way to Rome,  
where he will live in a religious community.” The event was seen in some  
quarters as another action by the USSR in an attempt to improve relations  
between the Vatican and Moscow. It followed an exchange of messages  
between Pope John XXIII and Khrushchev on the Pope’s most recent birth-  
day and on other occasions.

Other sources pointed to two other developments to help explain the sur-

to the Second Vatican Ecumenical Council last October followed the visit to  
Moscow of Msgr. John Willebrands, S.J., of the Secretariat to Promote  
Christian Unity. These initial contacts, it is believed, may have led to new  
results, including the release of Archbishop Slipy.  
Another development was the stand taken by 15 Ukrainian Catholic bishops  
of the free world attending the Ecumenical Council, who denounced the pres-  
ence of the two Russian Orthodox churchmen while Archbishop Slipy was still in  
a Soviet jail. Their protest may have started a chain reaction which led to the  
release of the Ukrainian Archbishop. Il Tempo of Rome, in discussing a possible  
reason for Archbishop Slipy’s release, said that Slipy early last year was offered  
the post of orthodox Patriarch of Moscow, but the Archbishop refused and sent a  
stern protest to the Soviet government over this “attempt at corruption.”  
It is recalled that on November 22, 1962, fifteen Ukrainian Archbishops and  
Bishops attending the Ecumenical Council in Rome issued a strong statement  
protesting the presence of two Russian Orthodox observers, contrasting their  
presence with the continued detention and persecution of Metropolitan Joseph  
Slipy. “The presence of the two Soviet observers at the Council has disconcerted  
true believers, astounded many Council fathers and engendered a feeling of dis-  
content and indignation among the faithful everywhere,” the statement said.

PHILADELPHIA, Pa. (Special) – On Sunday, September 8, 1963, the bless-  
ing and dedication of the new Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral took place here with  
an impressive ceremony, attended by some 3,000 faithful and 50 Ukrainian  
Catholic priests from the archdiocese. The act of blessing was performed by the  
Most Rev. Ambrose Senyshyn, OSBM, Archbishop of Philadelphia and  
Metropolitan of the Ukrainian Catholic Church in the United States.  
After the moleben an impressive procession marched to the site of the  
new cathedral headed by the units of Ukrainian youth organizations such as  
Plast and SUMA in their uniforms, and by representatives of Ukrainian cen-  
tral organizations, members of the Providence Association, the “Soyuz  
Ukrainok” and the local post of the Catholic War Veterans, as well as school  
children led by the nuns. The moleben was officiated by Metropolitan
214

Senyshyn, who was assisted by Rev. M. Charyna and Rev. William Losten.  
Metropolitan Senyshyn delivered an inspiring and penetrating sermon, in  
which he underscored the historical significance of Philadelphia, a “City of  
Brotherly Love” and the cradle of American independence, where such promi-  
nent Americans as Betsy Ross, Benjamin Franklin, George Washington and  
Thomas Jefferson lived and planned the foundation of the American republic.  
Philadelphia also has a special significance for Ukrainians, Metropolitan  
Senyshyn continued. It was here that the first foundations of the Ukrainian  
Catholic Church in the United States were laid down by Bishop Soter  
Ortynsky and his successor, Metropolitan Constantine Bohachevsky. In con-  
clusion, the Metropolitan bestowed his blessings upon those in attendance.  
Among the representatives of Ukrainian organizations taking part in the  
ceremony were Monsignor Stephen Cehansky, president of the Providence  
Association of Ukrainian Catholics; Stepan Sprynsky and Teofil Kulchytsky,  
recording secretary and financial secretary of the Providence Association,  
respectively; Joseph Lesawyer, supreme president of the UNA; Prof. Roman  
Smal-Stocki, president of the Shevchenko Scientific Society, Mrs. Helen  
Lototsky, president of “Soyuz Ukrainok”; as well as Eugene Zyblikevych and  
Mstyslav Dolnytsky, editors of America, and Anthony Dragan, editor of Svoboda.  
Plans for the new Ukrainian Catholic Cathedral, which will cost about  
$3,000,000, were drawn by Julian Jastremsky, prominent Ukrainian American  
architect, who was also present at the blessing and dedication ceremonies.

Title: Pathfinder club leaders train for OneVoice27 in Ukraine
Chunks: 0
Fifty-two Pathfinder club leaders in Ukraine met in Kamianets-Podilskyi on September 23–27 for a "One Voice" training session.
The training focused on the value of Children's Ministry and the responsibility of Children's Ministry leaders in preparation for OneVoice27.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The training program covered various aspects of a leader's work.
Speakers included Ivan Romaniuk, (“Creativity on a Budget”), Valerii Glushchenko, (“Mission Through Events”), Yevhen Alokhin, (“Building a Team That Avoids Burnout”), Valentyna Holoskevych, (“A Club Where Everyone Wants to Stay”), and Yurii Zhebet, (“A Year Without Last-Minute Rushes”).
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The workshops "Discipline Without Humiliation" by Pylyp Shubert, "Speak so They Listen" by Stepan Kumchak, "Understanding Each Child" by Nelia Perepylytsia, and "Worship Without Boredom" by Oleksandr Pecherskyi covered issues related to discipline, communication, and working with children.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Beyond the classroom, participants took part in activities designed to strengthen teamwork and build connections among leaders from different regions.
Attendees participated in "History of Faith," a walk through the streets of Kamianets-Podilskyi. Working in teams, attendees completed tasks and solved puzzles as they got acquainted with the city's historical sites.
After several days of intensive training, attendees went to Bakota to kayak the Dniester Reservoir for rest and informal discussion.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Participants said the combination of practical workshops, shared activities, and recreation helped them discover new approaches to ministry, exchange ideas, and build relationships with fellow Pathfinder leaders.
_The_ _original article_ _was published on the Ukrainian Union Conference_ _news site_ _._

Title: Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
While commanding both the Ground Forces and the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group, 80% to 90% of frontline defense already relied on unmanned systems, says Drapatyi. As commander, he repeatedly described the Drone Line as an example of how timely decisions can rapidly change the battlefield and demonstrate the military’s ability to drive innovation.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
Born in 1982 in Kamianets-Podilskyi, Drapatyi graduated from the Kharkiv Institute of Tank Troops in 2004 and began his career as a lieutenant in the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade.
When the Anti-Terrorist Operation (ATO) began in 2014, Drapatyi—then a major—commanded the brigade’s 2nd Mechanized Battalion. The battles for Mariupol made him a symbol of Ukraine’s resistance during the early years of the war in Donbas. In August 2016, he took command of the 58th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade. Even before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Drapatyi had advanced from battalion commander to brigade commander—not from headquarters, but while serving on the front lines.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Drapatyi was already serving in a senior command role. On March 17, 2022, he was appointed commander of the Southern Group of Troops, which was later reorganized into the Kakhovka Operational Group.
Under his command, Ukrainian forces halted the Russian advance toward Kryvyi Rih during the war’s most critical early weeks before launching a counteroffensive that pushed the front line forward by 6 to 23 kilometers and liberated dozens of settlements in the Kherson and Dnipropetrovsk regions. It was one of the defining turning points of 2022. Drapatyi remained in command of the Kherson grouping until 2024, meaning that the operation that ultimately liberated the west bank of the Kherson region was planned and executed under his headquarters.
Two men stand on atop a car with a poster "Kherson was waiting for the Armed Forces of Ukraine" during the celebration of the city's liberation on November 12, 2022 in Kherson, Ukraine. Kherson, which had been under Russian occupation since March, was liberated on November 11 as result of a counteroffensive by Ukrainian forces in the south. (Photo by Yevhenii Zavhorodnii/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
In May 2024, after Russia opened a new front with its offensive into the Kharkiv region, Drapatyi was appointed commander of the Kharkiv Operational Tactical Group. His mission was straightforward: prevent Russia from expanding its breakthrough into anything larger than a limited cross-border operation. Ukrainian troops under his command contained Russian forces within two small buffer zones along the border, preventing them from approaching Kharkiv itself or advancing deeper into the region.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## How Mykhailo Drapatyi reformed Ukraine’s Ground Forces
On November 29, 2024, Drapatyi became commander of Ukraine’s Ground Forces—the largest branch of the Armed Forces. By his own account, he inherited “an atmosphere of fear, a lack of initiative, resistance to feedback, and indifference toward the problems facing personnel.”
In response, Drapatyi replaced roughly half of his senior leadership team, launched reforms of the recruitment system aimed at combating corruption, updated training methods to better reflect the realities of the battlefield, and began integrating modern technologies directly into military instruction. The goal was a systemic overhaul of a personnel system that, for decades, had been built on personal connections rather than performance.
On January 26, 2025, Drapatyi’s responsibilities expanded further when he was also appointed commander of the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group—the largest operational grouping within the Ukrainian Armed Forces, responsible for the entire eastern front, from Velyka Novosilka in the Donetsk region to Kharkiv. President Zelenskyy explained that the decision was intended to strengthen the command structure along the war’s most intense sectors.
In June 2025, Drapatyi was appointed commander of Ukraine’s Joint Forces.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Challenges facing Ukraine’s new Commander-in-Chief
President Zelenskyy has made clear what he expects from the new commander-in-chief: preparing for Russia’s anticipated autumn offensive campaign and the possibility that the Kremlin could mobilize vast additional manpower. Ukraine’s military must be ready to halt any new Russian offensive and preserve the gains it has already achieved.
At the same time, significant reforms remain necessary within the armed forces, alongside efforts to strengthen the military overall, including through the wider adoption of new technologies.
“We all share the same goal: victory over the enemy and achieving conditions on the battlefield—and through pressure on Russia—that will force Russia to make peace,” said Zelenskyy.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
Born in 1982 in Kamianets-Podilskyi, Drapatyi graduated from the Kharkiv Institute of Tank Troops in 2004 and began his career as a lieutenant in the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade.
When the Anti-Terrorist Operation (ATO) began in 2014, Drapatyi—then a major—commanded the brigade’s 2nd Mechanized Battalion. The battles for Mariupol made him a symbol of Ukraine’s resistance during the early years of the war in Donbas. In August 2016, he took command of the 58th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade. Even before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Drapatyi had advanced from battalion commander to brigade commander—not from headquarters, but while serving on the front lines.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Drapatyi was already serving in a senior command role. On March 17, 2022, he was appointed commander of the Southern Group of Troops, which was later reorganized into the Kakhovka Operational Group.
Under his command, Ukrainian forces halted the Russian advance toward Kryvyi Rih during the war’s most critical early weeks before launching a counteroffensive that pushed the front line forward by 6 to 23 kilometers and liberated dozens of settlements in the Kherson and Dnipropetrovsk regions. It was one of the defining turning points of 2022. Drapatyi remained in command of the Kherson grouping until 2024, meaning that the operation that ultimately liberated the west bank of the Kherson region was planned and executed under his headquarters.
Two men stand on atop a car with a poster "Kherson was waiting for the Armed Forces of Ukraine" during the celebration of the city's liberation on November 12, 2022 in Kherson, Ukraine. Kherson, which had been under Russian occupation since March, was liberated on November 11 as result of a counteroffensive by Ukrainian forces in the south. (Photo by Yevhenii Zavhorodnii/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
In May 2024, after Russia opened a new front with its offensive into the Kharkiv region, Drapatyi was appointed commander of the Kharkiv Operational Tactical Group. His mission was straightforward: prevent Russia from expanding its breakthrough into anything larger than a limited cross-border operation. Ukrainian troops under his command contained Russian forces within two small buffer zones along the border, preventing them from approaching Kharkiv itself or advancing deeper into the region.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## How Mykhailo Drapatyi reformed Ukraine’s Ground Forces
On November 29, 2024, Drapatyi became commander of Ukraine’s Ground Forces—the largest branch of the Armed Forces. By his own account, he inherited “an atmosphere of fear, a lack of initiative, resistance to feedback, and indifference toward the problems facing personnel.”
In response, Drapatyi replaced roughly half of his senior leadership team, launched reforms of the recruitment system aimed at combating corruption, updated training methods to better reflect the realities of the battlefield, and began integrating modern technologies directly into military instruction. The goal was a systemic overhaul of a personnel system that, for decades, had been built on personal connections rather than performance.
On January 26, 2025, Drapatyi’s responsibilities expanded further when he was also appointed commander of the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group—the largest operational grouping within the Ukrainian Armed Forces, responsible for the entire eastern front, from Velyka Novosilka in the Donetsk region to Kharkiv. President Zelenskyy explained that the decision was intended to strengthen the command structure along the war’s most intense sectors.
In June 2025, Drapatyi was appointed commander of Ukraine’s Joint Forces.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Challenges facing Ukraine’s new Commander-in-Chief
President Zelenskyy has made clear what he expects from the new commander-in-chief: preparing for Russia’s anticipated autumn offensive campaign and the possibility that the Kremlin could mobilize vast additional manpower. Ukraine’s military must be ready to halt any new Russian offensive and preserve the gains it has already achieved.
At the same time, significant reforms remain necessary within the armed forces, alongside efforts to strengthen the military overall, including through the wider adoption of new technologies.
“We all share the same goal: victory over the enemy and achieving conditions on the battlefield—and through pressure on Russia—that will force Russia to make peace,” said Zelenskyy.

Fifty-two Pathfinder club leaders in Ukraine met in Kamianets-Podilskyi on September 23–27 for a "One Voice" training session.
The training focused on the value of Children's Ministry and the responsibility of Children's Ministry leaders in preparation for OneVoice27.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The training program covered various aspects of a leader's work.
Speakers included Ivan Romaniuk, (“Creativity on a Budget”), Valerii Glushchenko, (“Mission Through Events”), Yevhen Alokhin, (“Building a Team That Avoids Burnout”), Valentyna Holoskevych, (“A Club Where Everyone Wants to Stay”), and Yurii Zhebet, (“A Year Without Last-Minute Rushes”).
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The workshops "Discipline Without Humiliation" by Pylyp Shubert, "Speak so They Listen" by Stepan Kumchak, "Understanding Each Child" by Nelia Perepylytsia, and "Worship Without Boredom" by Oleksandr Pecherskyi covered issues related to discipline, communication, and working with children.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Beyond the classroom, participants took part in activities designed to strengthen teamwork and build connections among leaders from different regions.
Attendees participated in "History of Faith," a walk through the streets of Kamianets-Podilskyi. Working in teams, attendees completed tasks and solved puzzles as they got acquainted with the city's historical sites.
After several days of intensive training, attendees went to Bakota to kayak the Dniester Reservoir for rest and informal discussion.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Participants said the combination of practical workshops, shared activities, and recreation helped them discover new approaches to ministry, exchange ideas, and build relationships with fellow Pathfinder leaders.
_The_ _original article_ _was published on the Ukrainian Union Conference_ _news site_ _._

While commanding both the Ground Forces and the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group, 80% to 90% of frontline defense already relied on unmanned systems, says Drapatyi.
