# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
Born in 1982 in Kamianets-Podilskyi, Drapatyi graduated from the Kharkiv Institute of Tank Troops in 2004 and began his career as a lieutenant in the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade.
When the Anti-Terrorist Operation (ATO) began in 2014, Drapatyi—then a major—commanded the brigade’s 2nd Mechanized Battalion. The battles for Mariupol made him a symbol of Ukraine’s resistance during the early years of the war in Donbas. In August 2016, he took command of the 58th Separate Motorized Infantry Brigade. Even before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Drapatyi had advanced from battalion commander to brigade commander—not from headquarters, but while serving on the front lines.
When Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Drapatyi was already serving in a senior command role. On March 17, 2022, he was appointed commander of the Southern Group of Troops, which was later reorganized into the Kakhovka Operational Group.
Under his command, Ukrainian forces halted the Russian advance toward Kryvyi Rih during the war’s most critical early weeks before launching a counteroffensive that pushed the front line forward by 6 to 23 kilometers and liberated dozens of settlements in the Kherson and Dnipropetrovsk regions. It was one of the defining turning points of 2022. Drapatyi remained in command of the Kherson grouping until 2024, meaning that the operation that ultimately liberated the west bank of the Kherson region was planned and executed under his headquarters.
Two men stand on atop a car with a poster "Kherson was waiting for the Armed Forces of Ukraine" during the celebration of the city's liberation on November 12, 2022 in Kherson, Ukraine. Kherson, which had been under Russian occupation since March, was liberated on November 11 as result of a counteroffensive by Ukrainian forces in the south. (Photo by Yevhenii Zavhorodnii/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Not a desk general—Mykhailo Drapatyi’s military career
In May 2024, after Russia opened a new front with its offensive into the Kharkiv region, Drapatyi was appointed commander of the Kharkiv Operational Tactical Group. His mission was straightforward: prevent Russia from expanding its breakthrough into anything larger than a limited cross-border operation. Ukrainian troops under his command contained Russian forces within two small buffer zones along the border, preventing them from approaching Kharkiv itself or advancing deeper into the region.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## How Mykhailo Drapatyi reformed Ukraine’s Ground Forces
On November 29, 2024, Drapatyi became commander of Ukraine’s Ground Forces—the largest branch of the Armed Forces. By his own account, he inherited “an atmosphere of fear, a lack of initiative, resistance to feedback, and indifference toward the problems facing personnel.”
In response, Drapatyi replaced roughly half of his senior leadership team, launched reforms of the recruitment system aimed at combating corruption, updated training methods to better reflect the realities of the battlefield, and began integrating modern technologies directly into military instruction. The goal was a systemic overhaul of a personnel system that, for decades, had been built on personal connections rather than performance.
On January 26, 2025, Drapatyi’s responsibilities expanded further when he was also appointed commander of the Khortytsia Operational-Strategic Group—the largest operational grouping within the Ukrainian Armed Forces, responsible for the entire eastern front, from Velyka Novosilka in the Donetsk region to Kharkiv. President Zelenskyy explained that the decision was intended to strengthen the command structure along the war’s most intense sectors.
In June 2025, Drapatyi was appointed commander of Ukraine’s Joint Forces.

# Who Is Mykhailo Drapatyi? Ukraine’s New Commander-in-Chief
## Challenges facing Ukraine’s new Commander-in-Chief
President Zelenskyy has made clear what he expects from the new commander-in-chief: preparing for Russia’s anticipated autumn offensive campaign and the possibility that the Kremlin could mobilize vast additional manpower. Ukraine’s military must be ready to halt any new Russian offensive and preserve the gains it has already achieved.
At the same time, significant reforms remain necessary within the armed forces, alongside efforts to strengthen the military overall, including through the wider adoption of new technologies.
“We all share the same goal: victory over the enemy and achieving conditions on the battlefield—and through pressure on Russia—that will force Russia to make peace,” said Zelenskyy.

Fifty-two Pathfinder club leaders in Ukraine met in Kamianets-Podilskyi on September 23–27 for a "One Voice" training session.
The training focused on the value of Children's Ministry and the responsibility of Children's Ministry leaders in preparation for OneVoice27.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The training program covered various aspects of a leader's work.
Speakers included Ivan Romaniuk, (“Creativity on a Budget”), Valerii Glushchenko, (“Mission Through Events”), Yevhen Alokhin, (“Building a Team That Avoids Burnout”), Valentyna Holoskevych, (“A Club Where Everyone Wants to Stay”), and Yurii Zhebet, (“A Year Without Last-Minute Rushes”).
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
The workshops "Discipline Without Humiliation" by Pylyp Shubert, "Speak so They Listen" by Stepan Kumchak, "Understanding Each Child" by Nelia Perepylytsia, and "Worship Without Boredom" by Oleksandr Pecherskyi covered issues related to discipline, communication, and working with children.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Beyond the classroom, participants took part in activities designed to strengthen teamwork and build connections among leaders from different regions.
Attendees participated in "History of Faith," a walk through the streets of Kamianets-Podilskyi. Working in teams, attendees completed tasks and solved puzzles as they got acquainted with the city's historical sites.
After several days of intensive training, attendees went to Bakota to kayak the Dniester Reservoir for rest and informal discussion.
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Photo: Kateryna Horniak, Anna Makarenko
Participants said the combination of practical workshops, shared activities, and recreation helped them discover new approaches to ministry, exchange ideas, and build relationships with fellow Pathfinder leaders.
